articles.title: Russian hacker group claims to have posted B.C. school district information on dark web
articles.summary: CBC News has discovered a hacked database stolen from the Burnaby School District on a dark web site run by a prominent shadowy ransomware group believed to be operating out of Russia.
articles.byline: Jason Proctor, Jodie Martinson, Jon Hernandez, Ivan Angelovski

image.caption: Qilin, a group believed to be based out of Russia, provides tools for hackers to commit ransomware attacks in exchange for a cut of extortion profits. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: A shadowy Russian ransomware group has posted screenshots on the dark web from what appears to be a database stolen from the Burnaby School District.

The group — which calls itself Qilin — claims to offer downloads of information allegedly taken during a massive data breach school officials have said included medical information, detailed learning assessments, and personal information about both staff and students.

items: Cybercriminals may have accessed medical diagnoses in Burnaby school district attack: officials

blocks.text: Qilin is renowned as a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) provider that offers tools and infrastructure to hackers anywhere in the world in exchange for a percentage of proceeds demanded from victims.

While CBC News has not downloaded the contents of the files themselves, the screenshot samples posted on the Qilin website contain school district letterhead and human resource categories attached to what appear to be bulky files of data.
'Harassment Investigations' and 'Discipline'

The September attack on the Burnaby School District raised alarms with parents and students who contacted CBC News concerned that children's data may be in the hands of cybercriminals bent on exploiting deeply personal information for profit.

Working with CBC's visual investigations team, CBC News located the database shortly after the school district warned parents in an email Tuesday that "the threat actor claims to have published files and information from this incident on the dark web."
Hackers breached computer systems belonging to the Burnaby School District in September. The information they stole has been posted to the dark web. (CBC News)
The files appear on Qilin's dark web site in what is effectively a multi-page listing of sets of data stolen from various agencies, companies and individuals worldwide.
According to the screenshots posted online, the files contain a terabyte worth of data and have allegedly been seen nearly 4,000 times since they were first posted publicly on Oct. 15.
Screenshots of the files include folders labelled "Harassment Investigations," "Discipline," "Payroll" and "Mental health and Wellness."
CBC News has not viewed the contents of the folders.
In a statement to CBC News, the Burnaby School District said it has shared "reliable information with staff and families as it becomes available."

"We have engaged an external expert to help confirm whether data from the Burnaby School District has in fact been posted on the dark web and, if so, the nature and extent of any affected information," the statement said.
Widespread concern
According to the school district, hackers gained access to the district's systems on Sept. 21. The perpetrators appear to have started posting information online almost immediately.

CBC News received numerous emails about the incident after district superintendent Karim Hachlaf wrote to families on Oct. 14 confirming that "files taken containing personal information were copied and stolen by the criminal parties responsible for the attack."

CBC's visual investigations team took this screenshot of the dark web site where data stolen from the Burnaby School District in September appears to have been posted. The site belongs to Qilin, a Russia-linked group that provides hackers with online tools in exchange for a cut of ransomware profits. (CBC News)

Hachlaf's note claimed "most of the information maintained by the district about students, parents and guardians remains secure" but noted that "some bus touring information, student intervention records and other student assessments" had been affected "in a limited and smaller number of cases."
The warning sparked widespread concern.
"Help, our school has compromised our children's identity," one parent wrote to CBC News in an email that contained a copy of Hachlaf's note.
"I am a current Grade 12 student in the Burnaby Schools District who's been affected," wrote one student.
"Currently students and families have received virtually no clear communication."
Crippling attacks on institutions

In recent years, Qilin has been tied to a series of crippling high-profile ransomware attacks — most notably a 2024 cyberattack on Britain's National Health Service that saw major London hospitals cancel operations and blood transfusions.
Just last month, Japanese authorities handed over a Russian national accused of being involved with Qilin in connection with a European ransomware attack to German authorities.
The files contain medical information, detailed learning assessments and personal information about both staff and students. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
Ransomware attacks on health-care services and school districts have risen around North America, with schools in the U.S and Canada being targeted.
More than 60 million students and nine million teachers in both countries were impacted by a data breach of educational software provider PowerSchool.

The Associated Press found files describing sexual assaults, private hospitalizations and parental abuse among troves of data dumped online by a ransomware group that demanded $1 million in exchange for 300,000 files stolen from a school district in Minneapolis.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security describes Qilin's business model as one in which "a core group of developers will sell or lease their ransomware variant to other threat actors, called affiliates; the core developers will support affiliates' deployment of their ransomware in exchange for upfront payment, subscription fees, a cut of profits, or all three."

According to a threat profile prepared by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in 2024, Qilin has been operating since 2022, likely originating from Russia. The threat profile claims Qilin was observed "recruiting affiliates on a hacking forum" in 2023.

"Qilin is known to target organizations in various countries and industries, including education, healthcare and critical services, with geographical regions targeted including Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, among others. The group's targeting appears to be opportunistic rather than targeted," the threat profile reads.

"Victims are directed to communicate with the attackers via dark web portals or encrypted messaging services, ensuring the attackers' anonymity and complicating law enforcement efforts to track interactions. Payments are demanded in cryptocurrencies … However, even after payment, there is no guarantee that victims will receive the decryption tools required to recover their data."
Seeking 'information they can use'

Chester Wisniewski, chief information security officer and director of Vancouver-based computer security firm Sophos, told CBC News that attacks on schools are particularly common at the start of the school year in September and October.

"They're vulnerable because they're serving a large portion of the public, and them being offline or unable to open the schools provides an enormous amount of public pressure to do something," Wisniewski said.

"Usually they're after payroll information, they're after medical and personal information they can use. They're trying to upset the staff and the parents of the students in the case of a school, to get them to apply pressure on the school to pay an extortion demand."

items: Central Okanagan students, staff targeted in cybersecurity breach

blocks.text: To that end, Wisniewski said the thieves "don't care about your kids' grades, but they might care about their disabilities, or their learning problems, or their behaviour problems, or sensitive information about the finances of the staff members that work in the school."
Wisniewski said the Burnaby School District is working with another firm to strengthen security. He added that the public should refrain from blaming the victim.
Despite the fears of parents, Wisniewski said past attacks on other school districts have rarely resulted in individual harm.

items: Cyberattack on Burnaby School District triggers widespread disruption, concerns about data leaks

blocks.text: "The odds of something happening to your child's information despite it being published on the dark web where criminals hang out — it's a pretty low risk," he said.
"But it's certainly something to be concerned about and take protective actions."

articles.title: Inflation surges to 7.8% in October 2026 as fuel prices, fares climb
articles.summary: This marks the second consecutive month of accelerating inflation, as pressure piles onto already-stretched consumer wallets

blocks.text: TRANSPORT. Public utility vehicles ply their routes in Manila on March 16, 2026.
Rappler
This marks the second consecutive month of accelerating inflation, as pressure piles onto already-stretched consumer wallets
MANILA, Philippines – Inflation sped up further for the second straight month as higher fuel, electricity, and transport prices squeezed households already struggling with the rising cost of living.
Inflation soared to 7.8% in October from 7.2% in September, the Philippine Statistics Authority said on Thursday, November 5. It stood at just 1.7% in October 2025.
The latest inflation figure brought average inflation from January to October to 5.6%, well above the government’s target range of 2% to 4%.

Ahead of the release, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) had projected October inflation to settle between 7.1% and 8.1%, citing higher domestic fuel prices, electricity rates, and transport fares.
October was also expected to capture more of the impact of transport fare increases implemented in late September, which were barely reflected in September’s inflation figures.

Filipinos are already feeling financially stretched. An October study by Organic Intelligence found that 45% of urban Filipinos said inflation had drained their motivation to get ahead, while 42% had borrowed money for essentials such as food and transportation.

The persistent price pressures have also pushed the BSP to tighten monetary policy. The central bank hiked its benchmark interest rate by a “jumbo” 50 basis points to 5.50%, its fourth consecutive increase in 2026.
BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. warned that inflation could accelerate further in the coming months due to oil prices, transport fares, and the potential effects of El Niño on food production.
The BSP forecasts inflation to average 6.1% in 2026 and 6% in 2027. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 8 DPWH personnel suspended over Surigao del Norte projects
articles.summary: The cases involve allegedly incomplete but fully paid projects in Surigao del Norte.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 8:05am
An undated photo of the Ombudsman office.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the six-month preventive suspension of eight Department of Public Works and Highways personnel over alleged irregularities in fully paid but substantially incomplete projects in Surigao del Norte.
In a six-page order released Wednesday, November 4, the anti-graft body suspended seven engineers and one accountant while administrative cases against them are pending.
The Ombudsman said their continued presence in office could allow them to influence the proceedings.
"Sufficient grounds exist to impose preventive suspension on Respondents," the order said.

"Without delving into the merits of the case and based on the evidence submitted by Complainant, the allegations against Respondents appear to be supported by strong evidence at this stage," it added.
The preventive suspension is not a finding of guilt and may remain in effect for up to six months while the cases are being resolved.
The Ombudsman's Field Investigation Office II filed administrative complaints for conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service, grave misconduct and serious dishonesty.
The complaints allege that the DPWH paid in full for substantially incomplete projects under the Surigao del Norte 1st District Engineering Office, causing financial prejudice to the government.
According to the Ombudsman, evidence submitted by the Independent Commission for Infrastructure included a list of projects reported as completed despite incomplete deliveries.
The following personnel were placed under preventive suspension:

articles.title: P.E.I. health minister admits doctor recruitment has been 'underwhelming'
articles.summary: There was no ambiguity on the challenges faced in Prince Edward Island's health-care system from the health minister Wednesday.

blocks.text: PEI·New
There was no ambiguity on the challenges faced in Prince Edward Island's health-care system from the health minister Wednesday.
'The idea that everyone is going to have their own practitioner … is just not realistic,' he added
‘Our recruitment has been underwhelming’ admits P.E.I. health minister of physician hiring
There was no ambiguity on the challenges faced in Prince Edward Island's health-care system from the health minister Wednesday in the legislature.

Responding to Liberal MLA Gord McNeilly asking about Islanders waiting for access to primary care, Health Minister Cory Deagle said things need to be done differently, adding "we can't just use the excuse that it's bad everywhere" and called recruitment "underwhelming."

"The idea that everyone is going to have their own practitioner … is just not realistic," Deagle said. "We have to affiliate to the entity," he added, meaning Islanders could be cared for by those on a team in a patient medical home.
"I think Health P.E.I. has made significant strides over the last eight months to do that … and we're going to see good progress coming in the months ahead."
Then-P.E.I. premier Dennis King in 2023 promised to eliminate the patient registry by April 2025. (Julien Lecacheur/Radio-Canada)

In 2023, then-premier Dennis King promised to eliminate the patient registry by April 2025 by having every Islander signed up for care with a doctor or nurse practitioner. However, more than 30,000 Islanders are still waiting.
An email from the province to CBC News states that so far in 2026, 24 additional physicians have been recruited, 18 of whom are specialists and six family doctors.
'One of the worst' for hip, knee waits

Answering questions Wednesday from Progressive Conservative Summerside-Wilmot MLA Tyler DesRoches about hip and knee replacement wait times, Deagle told question period "it's not good," and said the province is "actually one of the worst within Canada."
According to the province's numbers, a wait can be more than two years.

items: UPEI patient medical home down to 2 nurse practitioners from 5
'Attached to a team': One patient medical home will take a new approach to Islanders' health care

blocks.text: "I do think that we can get to a place where everyone either has a family physician or is affiliated to a patient medical home, which is the model we want to move towards, which is the UPEI patient medical home," Deagle told CBC News outside of question period.

"I think we can make good progress in that. I think we're doing that at UPEI. This is not something that's being experimented on. It's done in provinces across Canada ... and it's how we're going to recruit physicians [and] nurse practitioners to P.E.I."
Deagle said the number of people on the patient registry has decreased by about 5,000 and some doctors have been recruited.
Default Caption: P.E.I. Health and Wellness Minister Cory Deagle was blunt about the challenges the province's health-care system is facing when questioned Wednesday. (P.E.I. Legislative Assembly)

He is confident patients can be connected with medical homes and said the UPEI patient medical home is not necessarily a new concept, though it is to the province, and changing a system doesn't necessarily come easily.

"What we've done over the summer is work with the medical society, the nurses' union, all the folks that are involved, to sit down with them and go over, how is this model going to work to affiliate to the building itself, to the patient medical home, not necessarily the prescriber," he said.

"I think those consultations have been excellent. For once, they actually feel like we're sitting down with them before we implement something to hear their feedback. And I think because of that and the trust that we've built up with these organizations, these groups, I think this can be successful at UPEI."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lucas McInnis is a journalist at CBC Prince Edward Island. He can be reached at lucas.mcinnis@cbc.ca.
With files from Wayne Thibodeau

articles.title: Milburn review to call for jobs ’revolution’ for young people with disabilities
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Government should introduce ‘flexi-jobs’ alongside subsidies and skills support, former minister will say

The British state should create and subsidise paid jobs…

blocks.text: The British state should create and subsidise paid jobs for thousands of disabled young people as part of an “opportunity revolution” aimed at reversing years of labour market discrimination, the Milburn review of youth employment will recommend.

The review, due to report this month, will say the government should introduce “flexi-jobs” alongside employment subsidies and intensive skills support to make it easier for disabled and chronically ill 16- to 24-year-olds to get work.

It will argue that the state should step in to underwrite jobs for young people who are locked out of employment and training opportunities, as part of an overhaul of what it sees as an outdated welfare and skills system.

About a million young people are now classified as “Neet”, meaning they are not in education, employment or training. Nearly half (45%) of those are disabled or in ill health. Disabled young people are three times as likely to be Neet as their non-disabled peers.

The review’s author, the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, has described soaring numbers of Neets as a moral and economic crisis, warning that failure to tackle rising youth disengagement from work risks creating a “lost generation”.

He has rejected what he has called “myths” about young people being “snowflakes”, insisting that the crisis in youth mental health is real, most youngsters want to work, and it is the duty of government and employers to provide support and opportunities.

The review will say young people with disabilities need a flexible and supportive approach to work that acknowledges fluctuating medical conditions and lack of work experience, and recognises the importance of part-time roles in helping them build confidence.

One eye-catching recommendation is for the UK to adopt a Danish-style “flexi-job” scheme. This guarantees disabled participants employment while allowing them to set working hours – in some cases starting with as few as four hours a week – that suit their individual capacities, with wages topped up by the government.

It will also call for creative ways of shaping jobs to individual capabilities, such as “job carving”: splitting the three component parts of a single entry-level role and matching youngsters to each of those roles. A retail role that comprises stock-filling, till work and locking up would become three job opportunities.

Nearly half of 24-year-old Neets have never worked, and Milburn argued in his interim report earlier this year that abandoning a cohort of Covid-era youngsters coping with high levels of depression, anxiety, autism and ADHD would have a scarring effect on their life chances and lifetime earnings.

Although the government has said it will not endorse “crude cuts” to benefits, Milburn has suggested that the state should switch some of the £4bn a year it spends on disability benefits for young people into comprehensive, high-quality employment and training support.

However, he will probably face pushback from campaigners, and potentially backbench Labour MPs, who argue that job support should not be funded by disability benefit cuts that would push many young people into poverty and further away from the job market.

Milburn’s proposals are in part a recognition that young people with disabilities face huge barriers around recruitment processes and inflexible job design, and many businesses are unlikely to create job opportunities for them without government support.

The plans have echoes of the postwar Remploy scheme, which created state-funded workplaces providing “sheltered” employment for disabled ex-service personnel. At its height, Remploy had 90 factories across the UK, the last closing in 2013.
The review will urge large employers to voluntarily adopt employment targets for disabled 16- to 24-year-olds, although it is expected to stop short of recommending statutory quotas.

As well as creating jobs, the review will call for a boost for job support, including supported internships, placements, specialist job matching and coaching, and support for employers to provide workplace adjustments.

Milburn who has been critical of the limited ambitions of existing government job support programmes, has previously called for a “turbo-charging” of specialist internships for young people with special educational needs who are moving on from school and college.

The most common conditions reported by disabled Neets were depression, bad nerves or anxiety (23.8%), followed by autism (22.7%) and other health problems or disabilities (18.5%), according to the latest official figures.

articles.summary: Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento has declined to testify as a witness for Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team in her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published November 5, 2026 7:52am
Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento has declined to testify as a witness for Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team in her impeachment trial.
In a video posted on Facebook, Sarmiento cited as reason the need to preserve his independence and impartiality as a constitutional law expert.

"I have decided to decline participation as a witness in the proceedings. This is a personal decision to preserve the independence of my constitutional law scholarship and the impartiality of my legal views and opinions," Sarmiento said in his post.
Sarmiento said he already communicated with Duterte's defense team to request the withdrawal of its subpoena request for his appearance before the Senate impeachment court.
If a subpoena has already been issued, he asked the defense team to seek its recall.
Sarmiento still thanked the defense team for recognizing the value of the constitutional and legal views he had shared on social media.
However, he pointed out that he had not anticipated that his opinions could potentially become part of the impeachment proceedings.
Duterte's defense team listed Sarmiento as its first witness in the unexplained wealth charges against the vice president.
On Wednesday, the defense team filed a request for a subpoena before the Senate impeachment court, with Sarmiento expected to take the witness stand on November 9.
Sarmiento is a professor of Political and Constitutional Law at the University of St. La Salle College of Law. He also previously served as the university's vice chancellor for administration.
He had earlier called for fairness in Duterte's impeachment trial following the prosecution's decision to drop three of the four charges against the vice president. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Unmanaged menopause symptoms cost Canada's economy $3.5B, experts tell MPs
articles.summary: Unmanaged menopause symptoms are not just impacting women, but costing the Canadian economy $3.5 billion and 540,000 lost workdays every year, according to the Menopause Foundation of Canada.

image.caption: Trish Barbato, left, and Janet Ko are co-founders of the Menopause Foundation of Canada. (Brenda Witmer/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics
Unmanaged menopause symptoms are not just impacting women, but costing the Canadian economy $3.5 billion and 540,000 lost workdays every year, according to the Menopause Foundation of Canada.
Health transition affects 25% of Canada's workforce, according to the Menopause Foundation of Canada
"Menopause is more than a health issue. It is a workforce issue, an economic issue and a public policy issue," said the foundation's co-founder and president Janet Ko.
"But women lose, too — $3.3 billion in income through reduced hours, lesser roles or leaving work altogether."

Ko and the foundation's other co-founder and director Trish Barbato spoke to the House of Commons committee on the status of women on Wednesday advocating for measures to improve working conditions and health care for women and people experiencing menopause.
"When the symptoms of menopause go unaddressed, they become a barrier to women reaching their full potential, and Canada pays the price," Ko said.
The first and most important priority, according to Barbato, is to train providers and make menopause education mandatory in medical training.

items: Years-long wait to see a gynecologist has N.S. woman considering care elsewhere

blocks.text: "This is the greatest barrier today for women. They cannot get the help they need," Barbato said. "Federally, we are asking for a national quality standard on menopause care."
Another high priority is supporting workers, according to the foundation.

"Employers are far ahead of other areas in our agenda because they have realized that supporting women during this period is not only the right thing to do, but it supports their bottom line," Barbato said.
According to Barbato, over 250 Canadian employers have signed on to the foundation's campaign "Menopause Works Here" including Sunlife, BMO, PWC, Ikea, Metrolinx and Horizon Health.
"Five million working women in Canada are over 40 … they are skilled, they are capable, they are experienced and a high-value cohort that employers cannot afford to lose," Barbato said.
"Yet more than half a million workdays are lost each year due to unmanaged symptoms."
Calls for workplace action plans

Barbato also suggested a review of benefit programs and ensuring coverage of hormonal and non-hormonal benefits for menopause, using the Bank of Montreal as an example — which has added enhancements including pelvic floor therapy.

The foundation also recommends that Canada follow in the United Kingdom's footsteps and make menopause inclusive workplace action plans mandatory for large employers. From early 2027, U.K. employers with over 250 employees will be required to publish a menopause action plan under the country's 2025 Employment Rights Act.

"Women over 40 make up one-quarter of Canada's population, and one-quarter of its workforce, the largest share in the nation's history," Ko said. "They are in their peak working years, but too many are reaching this stage without the information, care and support they need to thrive."
Committee MPs recounted their own experiences with menopause and perimenopause after the founders' testimonies.

"You're entering menopause at the same time you're really becoming at the top of your career, and that could be attributed to burnout in a lot of cases," said Conservative MP Kelly DeRidder. "I'm actually starting to question myself: am I burnt out or am I going through menopause? I don't know."
Conservative MP Anna Roberts said she had lost count of the number of years she's gone through menopause.

Liberal MP Marie-Gabrielle Ménard referenced the research of Dr. Kevin Whittingstall, director of the Université de Sherbrooke's medical imaging and radiation sciences department, which was presented to the committee at an earlier meeting in late October.
Whittingstall told the committee menopause increases the risk of strokes, cognitive decline and dementia.

items: 'We can’t deal with it in Canada': Some women turn to Mexico for endometriosis care

blocks.text: "Yet despite affecting virtually every woman, menopause has received only a fraction of the scientific attention devoted to other major health conditions," Whittingstall said, citing how diabetes research in Canada has received roughly $300 million in the past 10 years, while menopause research has only received $20 million.
Whittingstall said he believes Canada has "all the expertise" to become a leader in the field.

"Certain countries have put a lot of effort into promoting brain research across menopause," Whittingstall said. "The interest is there. It's Canada's turn to show we can do just as well, if not better."
According to Barbato, the numbers tell a story that has been a "part of the taboo and stigma" that comes with talking about menopause.
"Women have just had to deal with this on their own, they felt very alone and they certainly were not bringing it up at work," Barbato said. "That stigma and difficulty still exists today.
"The burden is on the woman. In her income, in her ability to have a Canada pension later in life, her retirement income, there is so much weight of that cost."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sophia Laporte is an intern with CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa and a fourth-year journalism and humanities student at Carleton University.

articles.title: Democrats take House and Senate from Republicans in US midterm rout
articles.summary: Democrats will control both chambers of Congress after flipping seats in Republican strongholds across the US in an election seen as a repudiation of President Donald Trump.

image.caption: Texas is sending a Democrat to the US Senate for the first time since 1988Image: Mike Segar/REUTERS

blocks.text: By late Tuesday night, it was clear that Democrats had succeeded in turning the 2026 US midterm elections into the so-called "blue wave" that had been predicted by pollsters.
But by Wednesday morning, the scale of the victory had turned into a "blue tsunami," surprising even the most optimistic political pundits.
In January, Democrats are set to have a commanding majority of at least 237 to 139 in the House and a 54 to 44 advantage in the Senate.
Democratic candidates flipped seven highly competitive Senate seats, including in what have for decades been reliably Republican districts in "red" states.
Texas voted in James Talarico as its first Democratic Senator since 1988, while electing a Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, for the first time in over 30 years.
The heartland state of Kansas, where farmers have been hit by high diesel prices and tariffs, will send a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in over 90 years.
Other surprise wins in Republican strongholds included Iowa, South Carolina, and Ohio.
Big Democrat victory in US midterm elections

According to data analyzed by the New York Times, the 2026 Democrats came in at a 13 point margin of victory over the Republicans for the popular vote in the House, the largest such margin since 1976 seen in the wake of the Watergate scandal that shattered the presidency of Republican Richard Nixon two years prior.

Democrats also saw large gains in almost every voter group compared with the 2024 presidential election that put Trump in the White House, indicating the breadth of the political swing away from Republicans.
The full scale of the Democrat majority in both chambers may not be known until later Wednesday or Thursday as some races are still too close to call, or take longer to count ballots.
Democrats promise change, buoyed by Trump's unpopularity
The midterms were seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump, who had historically low approval ratings of around 38% ahead of election day.
Trump had campaigned relentlessly in the weeks leading up to the election, in what often turned into meandering speeches to dwindling crowds.

Democrats were able to capitalize on Trump's unpopular policies like the war in Iran and ensuing record-high fuel costs, which compounded a growing affordability crisis while the president was seen as enriching himself.
On Wednesday, Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said his party was focusing "relentlessly on affordability and on accountability."

"The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over," said Jeffries, who could become the first Black speaker of the House in January.
Democrats say they are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower costs for fuel, groceries and healthcare, while conducting vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration.
When asked about the option of impeaching Trump or cabinet members for breaking laws while in office, Jeffries said Democrats were not focusing on that for now.
The margin of victory in the Senate is still not a two-thirds supermajority, with which Democrats alone could vote to convict in cases of impeachment, or override presidential vetoes.
Even as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term, Trump still has the power of the executive at his disposal, which comes with broad sway, especially in foreign policy.
Midterms put US political divide on display
GOP blame game begins

Despite for months claiming that Democrats would cheat to win the election, Trump did not dispute the Republican blowout. Instead, he claimed that Republicans would have won had his name been on the ballot.
Nevertheless, Trump said he would be willing to work with Democrats, while at the same time promised to use veto power to block legislation.
In remarks on Wednesday outside of his ballroom construction site at the White House, Trump appeared to admit that the economic impacts of the Iran war had cost the Republican Party.

blocks.caption: Trump preferred to speak more about ballroom project than the midterms on WednesdayImage: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

blocks.text: "I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term," Trump said.
Earlier Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance was more direct, saying the Iran war was the "reason we lost."
However, Trump spent the majority of the time in front of reporters on Wednesday talking about his ballroom project.
"It's going to be not only one of the biggest, but it'll be the most beautiful ballroom I think anywhere in the world," he said.
Republican supporters react: People are voting out of 'anger'

articles.title: Sara impeachment foes in Congress get scraps in proposed 2027 budget
articles.summary: Tweny-eight of the 36 district lawmakers who are poised to get the smallest public works budgets for 2027 either objected to the impeachment of the Vice President or abstained from the vote

blocks.text: Graphics by Nico Villarete/Rappler
Tweny-eight of the 36 district lawmakers who are poised to get the smallest public works budgets for 2027 either objected to the impeachment of the Vice President or abstained from the vote

items: The National Unity Party urged the House majority not to retaliate against lawmakers who opposed the impeachment of Vice President Sara Duterte, but many lawmakers who did not support the impeachment received significantly smaller public works budgets for 2027.

In contrast, lawmakers involved in prosecuting the Vice President are receiving much larger allocations, highlighting potential patronage politics and raising concerns about the transparency of the budget process.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Ahead of the House vote on the second impeachment case of Sara Duterte earlier this year, the National Unity Party called on the House majority not to retaliate against lawmakers who will not support their battle against the Vice President.
That appeal appears to have fallen on deaf ears, going by the proposed 2027 national budget.

Rappler’s analysis of public works funding allocations for congressional districts, based on aggregated data from People’s Budget Coalition and BetterGov.PH, indicate that congressmen who didn’t take a stand against the Vice President tended to receive smaller budgets for the upcoming fiscal year.

blocks.caption: How to track insertions in House-approved 2027 budget

blocks.text: Our review found that 28 out of 36 district lawmakers who did not vote to impeach the veep are poised to receive no more than P300 million each in Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) project funding for 2027.

From this number, 13 cast a no vote on Duterte’s impeachment. They include father-and-son Paolo and Omar Duterte, Southern Leyte 1st District Representative and Duterte-era public works chief Roger Mercado, and a handful of Mindanaoan lawmakers, such as Dal Corvera of Agusan del Norte, Laarni Roque of Bukidnon, Isidro Ungab of Davao City, and Nelson Dayanghirang of Davao Oriental.

Two specifically voted to abstain, namely Steve Solon of Sarangani and Audrey Zubiri of Bukidnon. Zubiri is the wife of current Senate Majority Leader Miguel Zubiri, who is seen by analysts as likely to vote in favor of Duterte’s conviction at the Senate.

Another 13 lawmakers did not vote at all. In Congress, legislators caught between opposing camps during contentious proceedings sometimes skip plenary sessions altogether, allowing them to avoid taking a position that could alienate either side.

A trio of lawmakers from Rizal who were absent during the vote — Jose Arturo Garcia, Tom Hernandez, and Emigdio Tanjuatco — are set to receive only P163 million for their shared engineering office in the proposed 2027 budget.

Even Deputy Speaker Kristine Meehan-Singson, despite her leadership role, had to deal with a smaller budget for her district. The Ilocos Sur congresswoman also skipped the May vote on Duterte’s impeachment.
At the bottom of the list is the engineering office that serves Davao City 2nd District Representative Omar Duterte, which received a measly P4.2 million in infrastructure funding for 2027.

The younger Duterte is the grandson of former president Rodrigo Duterte and son of incumbent Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, whose engineering office received the third lowest public works budget at P5.2 million.
The two Dutertes are often either absent or non-participating members during key House deliberations, but took the time to cast their no vote to the impeachment of the Vice President.
It is important to note that the figures could be higher. The budget watchdogs’ computation is still conservative, taking into account only projects handled by district engineering offices.
In reality, the budget for some public works projects is sourced from the regional or central office of DPWH. Lawmakers do not necessarily have control over all of these projects.
Some engineering offices serving the districts of lawmakers tapped to prosecute the Vice President at her impeachment trial fared better in the 2027 budget.

Most notably, the district engineering office that lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro shares with another Batangas congresswoman is poised to receive at least P3.1 billion in public works funds for 2027, putting her in the top 20.

The engineering offices associated with the districts of prosecutors Joel Chua and Bel Zamora are also getting more than a billion pesos in funding each, while lawmakers Lorenz Defensor, Lordan Suan, and Kaka Bag-ao’s associated engineering offices are poised to receive more than half a billion pesos in infrastructure funds.

In Congress, where patronage politics runs deep, it is not unusual for allies of the administration to get a bigger slice of the pie. In fact, the top beneficiaries of public works funds in the 2027 budget, based on the watchdogs’ computation, include Sandro Marcos, Speaker Bojie Dy, and appropriations chair Mika Suansing.

But the House has attracted growing scrutiny over its supposed failure to make the budget process in the lower chamber transparent, and to properly explain billions of pesos in adjustments it made in the President’s National Expenditure Program through the House spending bill.

The finding also comes on the heels of the Vice President’s concerns that the 2027 budget could be weaponized to pressure senator-judges into voting a certain way in her trial. Senator-judges have already pushed back against the allegation. – Rappler.com

articles.title: David Jones goes into administration, with store closures expected and thousands of jobs at risk
articles.summary:
Future of department store in jeopardy after administrators appointed on Thursday morning

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: Australia’s premier upmarket department store David Jones has collapsed into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk and leaving the future of the 188-year-old retailer hanging in the balance.

The upheaval follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent, culminating in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group.

Staff were informed on Thursday that the David Jones board had appointed voluntary administrators from McGrathNicol, before the retailer’s main financier promptly installed FTI Consulting as receivers.
Under the dual appointment, FTI will take day-to-day control of operations, running the department store network while it restructures the business.
The process will almost certainly trigger immediate store closures, though receivers will try keep the core network open while hunting for fresh capital.
David Jones employs more than 6,000 staff across a network of 38 stores.

articles.title: An Afghan teen won a full scholarship to a B.C. school. But Canada denied her study permit
articles.summary: Immigrant advocates say Canada regularly rejects study permits from Afghan women and girls, even when they have full scholarships, despite the fact that they face some of the strictest barriers to…

image.caption: Afghan primary school girls attend class at a school in Kandahar on Sept. 7, 2025. Advocacy organizations say Canada is denying Afghan women and girls opportunities to study in Canada, despite a Taliban ban that bars them from pursuing secondary or higher education at home. (Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Gett

blocks.text: After four years of being banned from the classroom in Afghanistan, a Kabul teenager was elated to win a full scholarship to a Canadian university prep school. Then her dreams came crashing down.
CBC is withholding the young woman's name for fear she could face retaliation for pursuing an education in defiance of Taliban law.

She was one of three Afghan teens selected out of thousands of applicants for a Canadian charity's education program. Then, in April, she was offered a two-year admission at a private boarding school in B.C., all expenses paid.

"When I first got my acceptance letter, my mind had made an entire new map, a new vision for me that could lead to my future," the 18-year-old old As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal. "I knew that all of my efforts had paid off."

But just a few months later, her hopes were dashed when Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) denied her study permit. Despite her full-ride scholarship, IRCC cited an inability to pay tuition among its reasons for rejecting her application.
IRCC declined to comment on the woman's case, citing privacy.
LISTEN | Interview with Kabul woman denied Canadian study permit:
As It Happens6:59An Afghan teen won a full scholarship to a B.C. school. But Canada denied her study permit
Her story is not unusual, say immigration advocates.

Multiple organizations told CBC that Canada has made a habit of rejecting study permits from Afghan women and girls, including those who have full scholarships, despite the fact that they face some of the strictest barriers to education in the world.
Advocate says gov't ignored scholarship

The Kabul student's scholarship was arranged by the non-profit Women Leaders of Tomorrow (WLOT), which partners with B.C. secondary schools to offer education opportunities to Afghan girls through its Empowering Limitless Minds program.
Of the three girls selected for the program this year, WLOT says two have been denied study permits, while the third remains in limbo.
WLOT executive director Friba Rezayee, a former Afghan Olympian, called the rejections "shocking."
She blames the Liberal government for reducing the number of international students it accepts to in 2024.

"The government has always said that they are standing in solidarity and support with Afghan women and they support human rights, democracy, and rule of law, and they also support girls' education," she said. "Then they deny their study permits."

Friba Rezayee, who is from Kabul, is the executive director of Women Leaders of Tomorrow, which arranges scholarships in Canada for Afghan girls to continue their secondary education. (Daryl Dick/The Canadian Press)
Rezayee says she believes the government is rejecting applications without thoroughly reading them.

In an IRCC letter to the Kabul teen, dated July 22, a case worker says the government denied her application, in part, because it was not convinced she would return to Afghanistan at the end of her stay, and because she had "insufficient funds/resources" to cover her tuition and cost of living in Canada.
But according to an April 27 acceptance letter from the B.C. school, she was granted a scholarship that covers tuition, school supplies, room and board, personal expenses and more.
"So they didn't even look at that," Rezayee said.

items: Girls are banned from Afghan schools. Secret networks are teaching them anyway

blocks.text: In an email to CBC, IRCC said all study permit applications "are considered on a case-by-case basis" based on the information provided.

It added that IRCC officers "examine files holistically" to determine "if they meet all program eligibility/admissibility requirements and if, on a balance of probabilities, the applicant is likely to respect Canada’s immigration laws and regulations."
There's still hope, says immigration lawyer
Immigration lawyer Gabrielle Thiboutot, who is not involved in the Kabul woman's case, says it's very plausible her application was not thoroughly vetted.
She noted IRCC uses automated software called Chinook to assess applications, and it could have missed the scholarship information.
CBC has asked the IRCC for information on how Chinook works and whether it could miss pertinent information.
Laurier grad is hoping her story will shine a light on education for girls in Afghanistan

Thiboutot sits on the board of directors for the advocacy group For The Refugees, which has run into similar roadblocks as WLOT. In 2024, two women the organization worked with were denied study permits to Canada, including one who had secured a $75,000 scholarship to Wilfrid Laurier University.

She says the IRCC argued the students would not return to Afghanistan at the end of their studies. This, despite that Parliament’s special committee on Afghanistan recommended in 2022 that the federal government issue study permits for Afghans with full Canadian scholarships “without assessing the intention of returning to their country of origin.”

But Thiboutot says For The Refugees successfully challenged the denied applications in federal court by arguing that even if the students don't go back to Afghanistan, their Canadian diplomas would open up opportunities for work or further study around the world.
She encouraged the prospective Kabul student not to give up hope.
"All the students we took on have arrived now," she said. "She won't make it for the semester … but the 'no' is not an end to her chance to come here for her studies."
Rezayee, however, says WLOT doesn't have the budget for a years-long legal battle.
"This message is directly to the prime minister, to Mark Carney," she said. "I need your attention on Afghan girls."
'It's not just about me anymore,' says scholarship teen
Speaking to CBC Radio from Kabul, the rejected applicant says this isn't the first obstacle she's had to overcome.
She still remembers 2022, when the Taliban banned girls in Afghanistan from attending school beyond Grade 6.
"I don't think I could ever forget," she said. "It was such a heavy moment."
Since then, she says, she's been taking courses in secret online. But she says the Canadian scholarship could be her last change to finish high school and carve out a better future for herself.

"I truly hope that they reconsider and review my application again," she said. "It's not just about me anymore. I have accepted this responsibility in my head to do this as a representation for all Afghan girls."

articles.title: Canadian military counterintelligence operative to face court martial in spy case
articles.summary: A Canadian military counterintelligence operative accused of sharing sensitive information with Ukrainian intelligence will face court martial beginning Dec. 9. Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar…

image.caption: Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar, a Canadian military counter-intelligence operative accused of passing sensitive information to a foreign entity, will face a court martial starting Dec. 9. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

A Canadian military counterintelligence operative accused of sharing sensitive information with Ukrainian intelligence will face court martial beginning Dec. 9. Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar faces three charges related to unauthorized dealings with a foreign entity, misleading his superiors and improperly storing a firearm. He was originally charged with eight offences.
Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar faces trial next month over alleged dealings with Ukrainian intelligence
A Canadian military counter-intelligence operative accused of passing sensitive information to a foreign entity will face a court martial next month.

Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar, who had originally been charged with eight offences under the National Defence Act, will be tried on three counts beginning Dec. 9, the office of the chief military judge said in a statement on Wednesday.
He was accused of communicating "special operational information" to a foreign entity, which was not identified at the time of his arrest almost a year ago.
A CBC News investigation at the time of his arrest reported that he was accused of passing sensitive information to Ukraine.

The three charges Robar now faces include negligent performance of a military duty, claiming that between September 2024 and February 2025 he had "an unauthorized relationship with a foreign entity and shared unauthorized information with that person."
The second charge is prejudice of good order and discipline, where he is accused of lying to his superior officers about the extent of his dealing with the foreign individual.
He's also charged with improperly storing a firearm.

items: Operative accused of leaking secrets was trying to help Ukraine: sources
How a Canadian military intelligence operative ended up facing an espionage charge
Case started with claims that Postmedia journalist is linked to Russia: sources

blocks.text: The statement from the chief military judge did not explain why the prosecutor is not moving forward on the other more serious charges, including communicating special operational information to a foreign entity and one count of breach of trust.
CBC News has confirmed through confidential sources that the individual to whom Robar is allegedly to have passed sensitive information was a representative of Ukraine’s defence intelligence agency.
He was introduced to that individual by another Canadian official and it is that association which is at the heart of the case against him.

Confidential sources told CBC News last year that the allegations against Robar stem from a Canadian military counterintelligence investigation into claims that a leading Canadian defence journalist was a longtime Russian asset.
The sources said Robar was tasked to look into claims that Postmedia journalist David Pugliese had been recruited by the KGB in the early 1980s.
Those sensational allegations were made in public before the House of Commons committee on public safety on Oct. 24, 2024, by former Conservative cabinet minister Chris Alexander.
A dossier of records purportedly from old KGB archives in Kyiv were tabled with the committee by Alexander.
Pugliese, a hard-charging journalist with the Ottawa Citizen, has exposed wrongdoing and mismanagement at the Department of National Defence for years.

items: Military intelligence operative accused of lying to superiors over Ukraine contacts
Canadian military intelligence operative accused of leaking secrets released from custody
Canadian military intelligence member charged with espionage, says DND

blocks.text: He has vehemently and repeatedly denied the allegations, including in his own appearance before the same Commons committee in 2024.

In an interview with CBC News last year, Pugliese said no one in the Canadian military contacted him and he had no idea a counterintelligence investigation was underway. He also said the seven-page dossier tabled in Parliament contains a number of errors.

According to two confidential sources, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the investigation, the dossier on Pugliese’s alleged Russian intelligence ties mysteriously surfaced in Eastern Europe in 2023 and Ukraine intelligence's directorate (DIU) was handed a copy.

Nothing in the dossier proves that Pugliese carried out any assignments for the KGB, the predecessor of the FSB, Russia's modern-day intelligence service — or that he was even aware of the apparent Soviet interest in him.
An independent researcher, who claims to have been fascinated by the case, produced a separate report, which claims the allegations against Pugliese were fabricated.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Code orange declared at hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie, B.C., after major bus crash

blocks.text: Code orange declared at hospitals in Mackenzie, Prince George
Police say multiple people have been injured in a bus crash on Highway 39 south of Mackenzie, a small community about 160 kilometres north of Prince George.
Northern Health says a code orange has been declared at both the local Mackenzie hospital and the University Hospital of Northern B.C. in Prince George in relation to the crash.
A code orange designation is declared for disaster or mass casualty events, and the term casualty applies to both injuries and deaths.
The health authority said it still doesn't have details to share on the number of patients or their conditions.
Health officials are asking people in Mackenzie and Prince George to avoid going to the hospitals’ emergency departments unless they are facing a life-threatening emergency.
The public has been asked to avoid the area of the crash, and Highway 39 is expected to be closed for several hours.

articles.title: Debt relief and aid no replacement for slavery reparations, UK told
articles.summary:
Leading figures in Caribbean reparatory justice movement speak out after UK PM announced infrastructure package

Offers of debt relief and development assistance from the UK cannot be a…

blocks.text: Offers of debt relief and development assistance from the UK cannot be a replacement for reparations for centuries of slavery, leading figures in the Caribbean reparatory justice movement have said.

Their comments follow British prime minister Andy Burnham’s announcement on Friday that he wanted to begin a structured dialogue on slavery and reparations and was open to Britain apologising, but ruled out reparations.
Instead, he proposed discussions on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

As leaders of the 56-member Commonwealth bloc meet in a private retreat at their summit in Antigua, Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement’s Repair Campaign, said that while countries in the region were likely to welcome Burnham’s offer, the Caribbean would resist any attempt to treat debt restructuring or development assistance as a form of reparation.

A 10-point plan drawn up by the Caribbean Community’s reparations commission, which outlines the region’s vision for reparations, specifically asks for “debt cancellation”- not debt restructuring – and “monetary compensation”, arguing that former colonies’ “existing debts are intergenerational and are ultimately and intimately tied to centuries of colonial extraction”.

“When I listened to Andy Burnham, and I listened to the king, and they’re talking about what is helpful is not reparations, but for them to work on specific things like debt relief, and education, and health, and climate change infrastructure.
“Now, all those things are within the 10-point plan. But they are also within the sustainable development goals of 2015, which we all signed on to at the United Nations,” he told the Guardian.

blocks.caption: Ralph Gonsalves said there were risks involved in reducing reparatory justice to development assistance. Photograph: Jeenah Moon/Reuters

blocks.text: He added: “There are things in the reparatory justice 10-point plan which deal with issues … the first one is the ecology, and then psychological repair. And for people like members of the Rastafari faith, or brothers and sisters who may wish repatriation, that’s something we have to work out with African countries, those who want to go back. But there are financial implications in that. So you’ll have to have a separate carve-out on the basis of the 10-point plan.”
Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, chair of the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations, said the question was fundamentally about “agency”.

Speaking at an event on Tuesday to launch a global reparations caravan, which will travel across countries to educate and engage people in the reparations movement, she said: “So when it comes now to reparative justice, and as we move forward in the movement, I have to be clear with everybody, it has to be about agency, not making deals here and there, because agency was the crime. When you think about what was taken from people of African descent when they were enslaved, it was their agency, their right to decide all of these different things about their lives.

“So when reparative justice arrangements are being made, it absolutely has to be made with those who were affected, because if it is done to us, it is not reparations. I don’t know what it is, but it is not reparative justice.”

Gonsalves said the danger of reducing reparatory justice to development assistance was that such assistance remained discretionary on the UK’s part. “We have to understand the specificities of reparatory justice as distinct from general sustainable development goals. They’re shaping the discussion only within the frame of sustainable development goals,” he said.

Prof Kingsley Abbott, a human rights lawyer and director of the Institute of Commonwealth Studies at the University of London, also stressed the importance of harmed communities having a decisive say in what reparations should entail.
after newsletter promotion

Speaking at the global reparations caravan launch on Tuesday, he said: “It’s for you to say. It’s your story. It’s your lived experience. But it’s time to start listening to those who continue to suffer from those crimes even today. It’s time to listen to you and to listen and learn from you.

“I reflected on my work as a human rights lawyer in different parts of the world. And in that time, I’ve met with many different victims of serious human rights violations, atrocity crimes, and their families and their descendants in places like Guatemala, Colombia, Nepal, Myanmar. And here in Antigua tonight, I’m meeting with all of you.

“Wherever those victims of those terrible crimes and their families were from, and whatever their faith, whatever their ethnicity, whatever their beliefs, they all had one thing in common. When I met with them, they all said that they wanted justice. And they wanted not only justice, but they wanted to be made whole again.”

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office said: “The prime minister wants to build stronger relationships to renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We will do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.

“We are already committed to working with Commonwealth partners on issues facing the world, including the role of private finance in tackling global debt issues, addressing the climate crisis, and supporting economic development. We will continue to do so.”

articles.title: Telstra apologises after customers mystified by phantom missed call notifications
articles.summary:
Telco blames its MessageBank service and apologises for customer confusion

  • Get our breaking news email,

blocks.text: Thousands of Telstra users have reported phantom calls on their mobile devices, with some receiving delayed missed call notifications or voicemails, sometimes days later.
The company acknowledged an issue with its MessageBank service on Wednesday night, saying the issue had been fixed.
“We identified an issue with our MessageBank service yesterday, which was fixed last night,” a Telstra spokesperson said in a statement.
“Some customers may have noticed several delayed missed call and voicemail notifications arriving at once, some dating back to several days.
“We’re sorry for the confusion this may have caused. There was no impact to Triple Zero calls, voice calls or mobile data.”
Telstra’s Facebook page received more than 3,000 comments from confused users.

“I got a missed call on my work mobile this afternoon from my personal mobile which was locked in my cupholder while driving and listening to an audio book via bluetooth,” LisaMaree Collier wrote. “No call on the call log of the private phone.
“So confused as I’ve not called myself in months (last time I misplace the phone).”
Another customer, Steven Alexandrou, said: “My dad was right next to me and my phone said he called me. I was wondering what was going on.”
A Telstra user named Simone Lou said the explanation seemed to be “why my boss called me after hours thinking I’d called him when I hadn’t 😑”.
Phil Richards also lamented the news: “Damn, I thought I was just really popular all of a sudden.”
Telstra has 26m mobile services on its network.

The company had a major nationwide outage in July that affected millions of customers, took some train services offline and prevented shops from using Eftpos machines. It blamed a “software defect” at the time, with CEO Vicki Brady saying Telstra would take the steps needed to prevent such an outage from happening again.

articles.title: National chief didn't mean to 'hurt anybody' with remarks on Métis identity

image.caption: Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak maintains 'pretendianism' — people falsely claiming to be Indigenous — is a widespread issue. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

The national chief who came under fire for her comments on Métis identity last week says she didn't want to "hurt anybody" but maintains there's a widespread issue of people falsely claiming to be Indigenous across Canada.
'You should be able to trace yourself back to First Nations people,' Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak maintains

When asked about the idea of abolishing the Indian Act on Oct. 26, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said there's "a big group" of Métis people who "probably have First Nations roots" in Canada.
First Nations need control over who can claim membership, as the federal government has had too much say for too long, the national chief said.
"There's a lot of confused people out there who are claiming to be Indigenous, a lot of pretendians, and then a whole group of everybody else who says, 'I'm Métis,'" she said.
"Can you trace yourself back to a First Nation?"

Métis leaders condemned the remarks, including Manitoba Métis Federation President David Chartrand, who called them "racist," as the Métis are included in Section 35 of Canada's Constitution, which recognizes and affirms Aboriginal rights.
CBC News asked Woodhouse Nepinak on Tuesday about Chartrand's response and whether she felt she misspoke.

"This is bigger than a Manitoba issue," she said. "This is a Canada-wide issue, and I think there is pretendianism, and there [are] box-checkers in educational institutions, in governments, in government contracting, in business development."

items: Infrastructure gap and specific claims top issues for Assembly of First Nations for federal budget

blocks.text: The national chief said Canada created the issue and must "rectify the wrongs" caused by the Indian Act, which dictates who is classified as a status Indian, as well as Bill S-2 — proposed federal legislation that would end the second-generation cutoff for Indian status eligibility.

Decried as "legislative extinction" and "definitional genocide,” the second-generation cutoff blocks children from acquiring Indian status when two consecutive generations of parents have a partner who is non-status.
"Deal with all of those issues first, on lands and the issues of membership with First Nations, before trying to dovetail into other groups of people in this country," Woodhouse Nepinak said.
The national chief said she did not intend to cause harm with her comments last week.
"It's the truth that there's a big problem in this country with identity and identity issues, with certain groups of people," she said.
"You should be able to trace yourself back to First Nations people…. I'll leave that there."
Indian Act discussion 'sideswiped' other issues

The national chief's initial remarks came as First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers met to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades. During that meeting, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew called for the Indian Act to be abolished.
On Tuesday, Woodhouse Nepinak also disputed claims by Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney that the idea to change or abolish the Indian Act was raised and supported by some chiefs in the room.
"No one" else brought up abolishing the Indian Act during the landmark meeting, the national chief said.

The chiefs involved had spent weeks preparing for the meeting and were focused more on the major projects legislation they say threatens their rights, but those conversations "went to the wayside" when Kinew and Carney made their remarks, she said.
"Those conversations can't be sideswiped just on one bombshell," Woodhouse Nepinak told reporters during a media scrum in Ottawa on Tuesday.
With files from Creeson Agecoutay and The Canadian Press

articles.title: UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns
articles.summary:
Minister hints at restriction on selling technology ‘to certain users’ amid worries over surreptitious filming of women

The government is considering placing restrictions on smart…

blocks.text: The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.
Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.

Kaur said: “The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.”
The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.

Kaur added: “Other settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.”

Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party who held Wednesday’s debate, said: “Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses.
“To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.”
after newsletter promotion

She said one of the selling points of the glasses in advertisements was that they could be used “to film discreetly”. Sabine said she did not want parliamentarians to “only regulate once it is too late”.

Kaur said smart glasses, which can come with built-in cameras, microphones and displays, could “be hugely beneficial” to some people. “For example, for those that are visually impaired, smart glasses have been a gamechanger, helping them navigate the world around them.”

A politician in the Senedd has defended his use of smart glasses in the debating chamber. Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, read a speech from an in-built teleprompter feature in his glasses last month.
He told the BBC’s Politics Wales: “One of the things I identified, a weakness of mine, was that my head was down looking at my notes a lot and I wanted to get away from that.”

articles.title: Serbia detains police officers over alleged use of force against protesters
articles.summary:
Interior ministry claims suspects tortured and intimidated protesters detained in garage of government compound

Serbian authorities detained nine active police officers and one former…

blocks.text: Serbian authorities detained nine active police officers and one former officer on Wednesday for ⁠allegedly using excessive force against detainees during anti-corruption protests last year in Belgrade, the country’s interior ministry ⁠said.

Anti-corruption protests swept ⁠across Serbia, ​a candidate for European Union membership, in 2025 and 2026 after 16 people died when a concrete canopy ⁠on a renovated railway station in the city of Novi Sad collapsed on 1 November 2024.

The protests ultimately ⁠resulted in the ouster of the populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is ​loyal to former president Aleksandar Vučić, in ‌an 25 October ‌snap parliamentary election by the leaderless Student List.

The ministry said in a ‌statement that the suspects, who served in an elite unit, tortured and intimidated several people detained in the garage of the government compound in downtown Belgrade on 14-15 August 2025.

“By the use of force and threats, (they) inflicted great pain and severe suffering on a larger ‌number of persons, intending to obtain information from them and intimidating and unlawfully punishing them,” the statement said.

The ministry provided ​only the initials of the officers and former officer who were detained. The news marked the first big arrests in connection with violence against the protesters who took to the streets over the past two years.
Police ⁠used teargas, crowd-control vehicles and stun grenades to disperse ​crowds during the ​protests.
Dozens of students and activists ​who took part in the protests accused police of ​excessive use of ‌force that ​resulted in injuries ​and psychological trauma.

Serbian students, activists, opposition politicians and rights watchdogs have accused Vučić and the SNS of political violence, pressure against media, ties to organised crime and rampant corruption. Vučić and his allies deny the accusations.
