articles.title: Sara Duterte's defense team lists law professor as its first witness
articles.summary: The defense team for Vice President Sara Duterte has listed law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento as its first witness in the unexplained wealth charges against her.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 1:06am
The defense team for Vice President Sara Duterte has listed law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento as its first witness in the unexplained wealth charges against her.
On Wednesday, Duterte’s defense team filed the request for a subpoena at the Senate impeachment court. Sarmiento is expected to take the witness stand on November 9.

“It is thus respectfully requested that this Honorable Court issue a Subpoena Ad Testificandum and Duces Tecum for said witness to appear, give testimony, and bring his Curriculum Vitae and other documents relevant to his qualifications and testimony, on said date. Dean Sarmiento will testify on legal and constitutional principles relevant to this impeachment case and on Article II,” the defense’s manifestation read.

According to the defense’s manifestation, the identities of the other witnesses to be presented will be disclosed five days before their intended hearing schedules on November 10, 11, 12, 13, 19, 20 and 23, as per the requirement of the court.
Sarmiento is a law professor of Political and Constitutional Law at the University of St. La Salle College of Law.
He is also the former Vice Chancellor for Administration at the University of St. La Salle.
Sarmiento also has a significant following online, with over 318,000 followers on Facebook.

He has previously called for fairness during Duterte's trial following the prosecution's decision to drop three out of the four charges against her. Sarmiento said that while it was important to hold Duterte accountable, there also needed to be fairness. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: US midterm results a 'victory' for Canadians hopeful of tariff relief
articles.summary: With Canada-US trade talks back on, Tuesday’s midterm Democratic wave puts pressure on the White House to come to a deal.

blocks.text: It was the midterm result that many in Canada had hoped for - a Democratic sweep that was in part a repudiation by American voters of Donald Trump's tariff on close trade allies.
"I was doing cartwheels down the street," said Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Wednesday morning, calling it "a victory for Canada".

Tuesday night's result is unlikely to grant Canada relief from those tariffs any time soon, but there is anticipation that the political shifts could create a more favourable environment for Ottawa to get the best deal now that on-again-off-again trade talks are back on.
US voters cited affordability as a main concern heading into the midterms and a survey by the Cato Institute in September, external suggested that about 75% believe the tariffs have raised prices.
In states like Maine and Michigan, tariffs played a significant role in the hard-fought races.
In Maine, incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins clashed with the White House over tariffs.
She successfully lobbied to have some duties that directly affected the state removed, including on road salt, refrigeration equipment and seaweed, but in the end lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

A similar story played out in Michigan, where state's the automobile manufacturing industry is deeply intertwined with Canada's - and where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.

Trump's 25% tariffs on non-US made cars and trucks have led to layoffs in the province of Ontario, and have contributed to thousands of dollars in additional household costs for Michiganders, according to an analysis by the US-based National Taxpayers Union Foundation, external.
Like Collins, Rogers sought to distance himself from Trump's tariffs, declaring in a TV ad last month that "Canada is not our enemy".
El-Sayed, meanwhile, bluntly assessed the tariffs as "dumb" and blamed them directly for driving up costs.
In Ohio, Senator-elect Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Jon Husted, called the levies a "disaster" and vowed to slash costs for voters by getting rid of them, external.
Democratic leaders like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, now newly empowered, have both pushed to rein in the tariffs on Canada in recent months.
Still, Democratic control of Congress might not do much to move the needle on tariffs. Trump's levies have been largely enacted using executive orders without approval from Congress.
And speaking to Fox News on Tuesday night, Trump touted his "ultimate power" of veto to shut down bills passed by Congress that he does not like.
Some Democratic lawmakers have also supported certain tariffs in the past as a way to protect American manufacturing jobs, and could back keeping some in place.
There are currently several layers of tariffs on Canada, notably on sectors like autos, steel, aluminium and forestry.

After trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed in August, the Trump administration imposed an additional 50% tariff on $20bn (£15bn) worth of various Canadian goods, from dairy to cosmetics and furniture.
The US also declared a total import ban on motorcycles, whey protein and alcohol.
Canada retaliated by slapping the US with its own 50% "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs. Most provinces have also banned the sale of US alcohol in retaliation.
Trump had also previously threatened to escalate the trade war with Canada further by ⁠raising tariffs on sectors, including auto manufacturing, as of 1 January.
There were signs that his administration had become more sensitive to the optics of its tariffs on Canada in the run up to the election.
Just a few days before the vote, Trump told reporters that a trade deal is "very close" after speaking with Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday evening, Carney said of US negotiators that "they're asking less and they're offering more" in recent discussions.

On Wednesday, US-Canada Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the midterm results won't change anything in the short term, and dismissed speculation over what the new Congress might do when they're seated in the new year as "an interesting discussion at a faculty club luncheon".
"Our approach will not change and we don't intend to speculate on the approach being taken by the Americans," he said.

Trump may feel more pressure to sign a deal with Canada now that American voters have clearly communicated their frustration, said Colin Robertson, a former Canadian diplomat and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.
"Will this change Trump's mind? It might, because he suffered such a beating at the polls."
But he added it remains to be seen how Trump will react from the bruising midterm loss.
Canada has an ideal window between now and January - when the new Democratic lawmakers are sworn in - to finalise a deal, Robertson noted.
After that, Trump is likely to be distracted by investigations launched by Democrats into Trump's family and finances and some members of his administration, Robertson said.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer also said earlier this year that he had ambitions to have interim deals in place with Canada and Mexico around the North American free trade deal, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada, before the end of the year.

And while Carney struck a more optimistic tone in recent days on the current state of Canada-US trade talks, he also told Politico last month that he was prepared to wait for a new American president if necessary to reach a deal with the US.

articles.title: ICC prosecutors cite Kian, Parojinog killings in bid to challenge police self-defense claims
articles.summary: International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors are seeking to introduce additional testimony citing several high-profile killings to challenge Philippine National Police (PNP) claims that officers…
articles.byline: JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN, ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 12:48am

International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors are seeking to introduce additional testimony citing several high-profile killings to challenge Philippine National Police (PNP) claims that officers acted in self-defense during former President Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war.
In its tenth application under Rule 68(3), made public on November 3, the Office of the Prosecutor asked Trial Chamber III to admit the prior recorded testimonies of witnesses P-0025 and P-1382.

The two witnesses, prosecutors said, provide evidence on the scale and circumstances of killings during Duterte’s drug war, including an increase in police killings, and discrepancies between evidence examined by the witnesses and police accounts of self-defense.

P-0025’s prior recorded testimony, which is a written statement on the witness’s four-day interview of a redacted individual, concerns around a hundred people killed by law enforcement in the context of “War on Drugs,” including victims linked to charged Incidents 14, 30, 46 and 55.

In the Prosecution’s Trial Brief, Incident 14 refers to the killing of former Ozamiz City Mayor Reynaldo Parojinog Sr. and several other individuals on July 30, 2017. Incident 30, meanwhile, refers to the killing of Kian delos Santos on August 16, 2017.

The victims of Incident 46 were two alleged drug users in Bulacan killed by “PNP personnel and a non-police hitman”, while the alleged drug user in Incident 55, which took place in Quezon City, was “shot and killed” by PNP personnel.

The filing says P-0025 describes material that “in several cases contradict[s] allegations of self-defense made by the police,” but some details behind those contradictions are redacted in the public version.

Prosecutors said P-0025’s testimony supports their allegation of a policy to “neutralize through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines,” as well as the alleged “widespread and systematic” nature of the crimes.
In the case of P-1382, substantial portions of the witness’ background and testimony are also redacted.

The public filing states that P-1382 provides evidence on a significant increase in killings during Duterte’s presidency and on police operations conducted amid that surge. It also says the witness is expected to testify about an instruction he received, but the substance of that instruction is redacted.
The prosecution said the accounts of P-0025 and P-1382 are cumulative and corroborate other expected evidence, including testimony from P-0009, P-1345, P-1359, and P-1162.
This latest filing is the prosecution’s ninth application so far under Rule 68(3).
Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity, involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed during his tenures as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.
His trial is set to begin on November 30 before ICC Trial Chamber III, composed of Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Tinto Brass, director of Caligula and maestro of Euro erotica, dies aged 93
articles.summary:
The cult Italian film-maker began as an assistant to Roberto Rossellini but moved into sex films, believing ‘eroticism to be a fundamental key to human expression’

Italian film director…

blocks.text: Italian film director Tinto Brass, who was once hailed as the “Antonioni of the 70s” but came to be better known for bringing Italian erotic cinema to a wider audience with films such as Caligula and Salon Kitty, has died aged 93.
His wife Caterina Varzi and children Bonifacio and Beatrice Brass announced the news of the director’s death to Italian press agency Ansa on Wednesday.

Born in Milan and raised in Venice, Brass first started working in cinema after moving to Paris, where he was an editor and archivist at the Cinémathèque. Upon returning to Italy, he worked as an editor and assistant director to Roberto Rossellini.

His experimental and anarchic approach to film quickly earned him a reputation, and in 1964 he was commissioned by Umberto Eco to create two short films experimenting with visual language for the Triennale di Milano. Warner Bros reportedly approached him to direct A Clockwork Orange, though scheduling conflicts meant the film was offered to Stanley Kubrick instead.

blocks.caption: Malcolm McDowell and Helen Mirren in Caligula. Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/Alamy

blocks.text: In the 1970s, Brass moved on to erotic cinema. Though crass and filled with nudity, his first steps in the genre were also politically minded explorations of the relationships between sex, power and money.

“I made so many erotic films because I believed eroticism to be a fundamental key to human expression and, above all, the key to portraying women,” he told La Repubblica newspaper. “That was what interested me most.”

His 1976 “Nazisploitation” film Salon Kitty was based on the true story of a Berlin brothel co-opted by Nazis to spy on foreign allies and fellow officers. It caught the attention of producer and Penthouse founder Bob Guccione, who hired Brass in 1979 to direct Caligula, which was an attempt to make a star-studded, mainstream pornographic film, with a plot based on the story of ancient Rome’s most feared ruler.

blocks.caption: Brass and the cast of one of his films at the Venice film festival in 1999.  Photograph: Graham Whitby-Boot/Sportsphoto/Allstar

blocks.text: Starring Malcolm McDowell in the title role, alongside Helen Mirren, Peter O’Toole and John Gielgud, the film was based on a screenplay by Gore Vidal, which Brass rewrote to include orgies, decorative phalluses, and plenty of female nudity.

Vidal disavowed the film, as did Brass after Guccione shot additional unsimulated hardcore sex scenes and spliced them into the film without the director’s permission. It was released in the UK and US in 1980, with Brass only credited for “principal photography”. A recut version, without Guccione’s inserts, was released in 2023, although Brass was not involved and did not approve of it.

In recent years Brass lived in Isola Farnese, on the outskirts of Rome. He is survived by his wife, Varzi, whom he married in 2017 and who curated his archive. In an interview on the occasion of his 90th birthday, he expressed a wish for his ashes to be scattered in the Venice lagoon.

articles.title: 'Most difficult days of my life' for keeper Owono
articles.summary: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono puts out a statement through his club, expressing his sorrow and pain after Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel's death.

blocks.text: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.
The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.
Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally".
"These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement.
"I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened.
"I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him.

"I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing.
"Rest in peace, Jesus."
Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.
Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.

Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone.
"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."
Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time on Monday when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him, before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.
The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player.
"As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.
On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.
Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.
The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.
Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell".

"Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the club statement.
Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

articles.title: The young politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
articles.summary: For some young Africans, these victories offer a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could do at home.

blocks.text: "JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".
It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.

Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.

The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations.

"My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.
El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.

The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.
But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.
The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.
At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.

Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.
Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.
Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.
Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.

She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests.
Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".
She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.

Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.
The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.

Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.
His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.
In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.
Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.

First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.

Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.
Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.
Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House.

Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.
For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.
On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

articles.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola to be evacuated from DRC to UK, document shows
articles.summary:
Patient, who is ⁠in ​stable condition, is expected to arrive in Britain on Wednesday or Thursday

A British healthcare worker infected with Ebola ⁠is being medically evacuated from the…

blocks.text: A British healthcare worker infected with Ebola ⁠is being medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Britain for specialist treatment, according to an official document seen by ⁠Reuters.

The patient is ⁠in a ​stable condition and is expected to arrive in Britain on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred to a specialist ambulance to ⁠a high-consequence infectious disease unit, the document showed.
It quoted British authorities saying they did not expect the case to have a serious public health ⁠impact in Britain, and anticipated no disruption to international travel or trade.

“A British citizen currently ​in the DRC has tested positive for ‌Ebola,” a spokesperson for ‌Britain’s government told Reuters in an emailed statement. “ … The risk to the UK public ‌from Ebola remains low.“
The patient, whose identity was not disclosed, had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help support the response to the outbreak.
It is the first case involving a British national linked to the current outbreak, although several other people from elsewhere in Europe have been infected.

Switzerland last month evacuated an Ebola patient ‌from Nigeria for treatment, while France in June reported its first confirmed case tied to the outbreak in a doctor returning from a humanitarian ​mission in DR Congo.

Ebola is a severe viral disease spread through direct contact with an infected person’s body fluids. The World Health Organization says the disease is fatal in about half of cases on average, though mortality rates vary between outbreaks.

British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the ​National Health Service has procedures ​in place to manage suspected ​and confirmed infections.
Imported cases are rare, with only four confirmed cases recorded in ​Britain since 1976, ‌according to the ​UK Health Security Agency.
The ​outbreak in DR Congo is the second-largest on record, with more than 10,000 confirmed cases and nearly 5,000 deaths reported by late October.

articles.title: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.summary: The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers.

blocks.text: French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.

Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.

But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.

"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.

In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.

"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.

"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
But no formal attribution has been made.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.
Additional reporting from Chris Vallance

articles.title: Kosovo: Outrage as authorities accused of not helping femicide victim
articles.summary: Despite reporting her husband to the police and pleading for protection, Arlinda Zekaj was brutally murdered. Now, thousands in Kosovo are protesting what they say is a dramatic failure of state…

image.caption: Protesters poured red paint onto a flight of steps outside the seat of Kosovo's government on the day after Arlinda Zekaj's murder. The banner behind them reads 'The state killed Arlinda' Image: Vjosa Cerkini/DW

blocks.text: Arlinda Zekaj repeatedly asked the Kosovo police for protection. They said she was exaggerating.

On October 25, the 49-year-old once again reported her husband to the police. This time, he was arrested. But Zekaj also asked the police for additional protection — this time against her husband's family. But to no avail.

The police drove Arlinda Zekaj home. Her killer was waiting. At 8:58 p.m., Zekaj got out of the squad car. A short time later, the police received an emergency call. When officers arrived at Zekaj's house at 9:10 p.m., they found only her body.
The 49-year-old had been brutally murdered in her bedroom with an axe. By that time, the alleged perpetrator — her brother-in-law, Albert Sylaj — had fled.
Protests across Kosovo

The murder, which took place in the village of Vitomirica, near the city of Peja in western Kosovo, has sparked numerous public protests and demonstrations involving thousands of people across the country.
It was the eighth femicide in Kosovo in 2026 — and apparently the most brutal.

More so than almost any other femicide in the country in recent years, Zekaj's death demonstrated that one of the things that made her killing possible was the fact that police and prosecutors ignored the victim's pleas for help .
Ministers refuse to resign
One of the first protests took place on October 26, when a group of feminists emptied buckets of red paint on steps outside the seat of Kosovo's government in the capital, Pristina.
"The state killed Arlinda," read a banner that the activists hung at the entrance to the building.

In the days that followed and on November 1, public anger brought thousands of people to streets across Kosovo. Many carried photographs of murdered women. One slogan appeared again and again: "The government has blood on its hands."
The protesters are demanding that charges be brought against the police officers and prosecutors responsible for handling Zekaj's case.

They are also calling for the resignation of Interior Minister Xhelal Svecla and Justice Minister Donika Gervalla, whom Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti appointed national coordinator for protection against domestic violence in March.
Both Svecla and Gervalla have rejected calls to step down.
For his part, however, Kurti acknowledged that certain Kosovo state institutions had "failed."
A murder foretold
In many ways, this was a murder foretold.

As far back as the summer, Arlinda Zekaj had reported her husband to the police for making threats against her. A court in Peja subsequently issued a protection order, granted her temporary custody of their son and gave her the right to remain in the family home.

The protection order allowed her husband to continue living in the same house, provided he did not come within two meters (about 6.5 feet) of her. Outside the home, he was required to keep a distance of at least 20 meters.
Zekaj had decided against moving to a women's shelter because she wanted to continue living in her own home with her son.
Even after the protection order was issued, she repeatedly made complaints to the police, among other things about threats from her brother-in-law Albert Sylaj.

Three days before the killing, on October 22, Zekaj reported that members of her husband's family, including Sylaj, were in her home against her wishes. According to her account, he threatened her with the words: "Leave or I'll kill you."
Nevertheless, Sylaj was questioned only as a witness in the case against Zekaj's husband.
Police arrested him near Peja on October 27. He is now under investigation for murder.
'A collapse of the state and society in relation to women'
Since 2010, 55 women in Kosovo have been killed by partners or family members, often after years of documented abuse and ignored complaints.
In recent years, successive Kosovo governments have adopted a number of laws and regulations aimed at better combating violence against women.
These measures include the possibility of life sentences for perpetrators in femicide cases.

Activists argue, however, that the authorities responsible for enforcing these measures — including police, social services, prosecutors and courts — have failed to implement them consistently and in a coordinated manner.

blocks.caption: Relations of Arlinda Zekaj, who was murdered in her home at the end of October, took part in a protest on October 28. One of the placards reads 'Mom, I love you very much' and shows a photo of the victim and her sonImage: Vjosa Cerkini/DW

blocks.text: Writing in an article for the news portal Nacionale, lawyer Njomeza Zejnullahu said that "After every murder, we hear the same word: failure. 'The institutions have failed.' I disagree. Failure is when something happens once, when a system that normally works breaks down at one point. When the cases keep repeating themselves, when the victims are almost always women and each of them had previously knocked on the door of an institution, it is no longer a failure. It is a collapse of the state and society in relation to women in general."
What needs to change?

In the aftermath of Arlinda Zekaj's killing, several senior police officers from Peja and the surrounding area have been suspended. A prosecutor who had handled Zekaj's complaints has also been suspended.
For the protesters in Kosovo, however, this is not nearly enough.

"All those involved within the chain of responsibility must not only be removed from office but also criminally prosecuted for failing to fulfil their official duties," said Liridona Sijarina, a political scientist and feminist activist with Kosovo's Kolektivi Feminist (Feminist Collective).
"That includes not only police officers, prosecutors and judges, but also Mayor of Peja Gazmend Muhaxheri and, ultimately, government ministers," she told DW.

Sijarina went on to say that feminist activists are also calling on the Interior Ministry to create a dedicated unit that would treat women's safety as a matter of national security and focus specifically on preventing femicides.

She also said that the government should make its draft legislation on affordable social housing a top political priority and ensure that women who have experienced domestic violence are eligible for social housing.

"In our view," said Sijarina, "the behavior of the institutions so far has deepened women's distrust of the state and, as a result, allowed violence against them to escalate. The government now has the opportunity to show whether it truly takes women's lives seriously by clearly responding to our demands."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Sara, Leni gap narrows – OCTA
articles.summary: The gap between Vice President Sara Duterte and Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo in a hypothetical presidential matchup in 2028 has narrowed to its closest in the latest OCTA Research group poll.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte and Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo
composite imag PNA / Joan Bondoc; The STAR / Noel Pabalate

MANILA, Philippines — The gap between Vice President Sara Duterte and Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo in a hypothetical presidential matchup in 2028 has narrowed to its closest in the latest OCTA Research group poll.
Based on the Sept. 28 to Oct. 4 survey, 40 percent of respondents said they would vote for Duterte if she ran against Robredo in a hypothetical one-on-one matchup in the 2028 presidential elections.
It dropped three points from the 43 percent she obtained in a similar survey in July.
Meanwhile, 33 percent said they would vote for Robredo.
In the previous poll, she obtained 34 percent.
Twenty-six percent were undecided, from 22 percent in the last survey.
According to OCTA, the gap between the two officials is now down to seven points, the lowest in the series of hypothetical matchups it conducted this year.

“VP Duterte’s seven-point lead is outside the plus/minus three-percent margin of error, and she leads in Class D, which carries the most weight in the national estimate, as well as in the Visayas and Mindanao,” the polling firm said.

“Her national share is lower in each of the three 2026 waves and the cumulative six-point difference is larger than the margin of error. This may indicate some softening in her support over the year, though three data points are not sufficient to establish a long-term trend,” it added.
The lower support for Duterte, however, did not translate to higher support for Robredo, with a sizeable bloc saying they were undecided if the two officials ran against each other.
Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Marcos is focused on more important issues affecting Filipinos rather than presidential surveys.

articles.title: New chief justice named this week
articles.summary: President Marcos will name this week the next chief justice to succeed Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who will retire tomorrow.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 12:00am
The President recognized Gesmundo’s public service and contributions to the country’s justice system.
Philstar.com / EC Toledo
MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos will name this week the next chief justice to succeed Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who will retire tomorrow.
This is the first time Marcos is picking the top magistrate.
Marcos yesterday conferred the Order of Lakandula with the Rank of Grand Cross (Bayani) on Gesmundo in a ceremony at Malacañang.
“Let us wait for the announcement of the next chief justice, which is expected this week,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said.
Gesmundo will reach the mandatory retirement age of 70 on Nov. 6.
Associate Justice Raul Villanueva was Marcos’ first appointee to the high court.
The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) has submitted a shortlist of nominees for chief justice and Supreme Court associate justice to the President.
The JBC said five SC justices were shortlisted for the chief justice position.

They are Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa, Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda, Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao and Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez.

Two other senior magistrates, Associate Justices Ramon Paul Hernando and Henri Jean Paul Inting, withdrew their acceptance of their nominations for the chief justice post before the shortlist was submitted.
New PTV GM
Meanwhile, the President has named John Benedict Teston Tigson as the new general manager of the People’s Television Network.
Presidential Communications Office Secretary Lino Cayetano yesterday administered the oath of office to Tigson.
Tigson replaced Cayetano, who was appointed PCO chief last month.

articles.title: Rules on absent senators sought
articles.summary: Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente Sotto III has filed a resolution seeking definitive rules to address the absences of senators like Ronald dela Rosa, who has gone into hiding since the…

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 12:00am

Sotto filed Senate Resolution 751 on Oct. 27 to address the policy gap in the Senate rules that allowed Dela Rosa to get away with being absent since the ICC issued the warrant for his arrest in November last year.
STAR / Geremy Pintolo, file

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente Sotto III has filed a resolution seeking definitive rules to address the absences of senators like Ronald dela Rosa, who has gone into hiding since the International Criminal Court (ICC) ordered his arrest for crimes against humanity.
Senate rules are silent on what to do with members who go absent without authorization, disrupting their legislative duties and wasting public funds, Sotto said.

“There is a policy gap as regards the possible sanction on a member of the Senate with prolonged unauthorized absence, rendering them unable to participate in major legislative functions,” Sotto said.
“Such absenteeism and neglect of duty is deemed a waste of taxpayer funds and has caused public clamor over the past months,” he said.
Sotto urged the Senate committee on rules “to institutionalize addressing the prolonged unauthorized absence of members of the Senate.”

articles.title: PNP: Personal ties won’t affect Bato manhunt
articles.summary: Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa’s past position as Philippine National Police chief has no bearing on efforts to arrest him, PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said yesterday.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa’s past position as Philippine National Police chief has no bearing on efforts to arrest him, PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said yesterday.
Nartatez maintained Dela Rosa’s personal relationships with his former subordinates would not influence efforts to enforce the arrest warrant against their former chief.
“The Philippine National Police will remain professional, impartial and steadfast in implementing lawful orders, regardless of who is involved,” he said in a statement.
Palace press officer Claire Castro on Tuesday challenged the PNP to ensure that Dela Rosa’s past stature in the PNP would not affect manhunt operations for him.
Nartatez welcomed Malacañang’s challenge, saying it reinforces a fundamental principle of law enforcement wherein no position, rank or personal relationship is above the law.
He said police officers are loyal to the Constitution and not to persons who previously held positions of authority like Dela Rosa.

Dela Rosa, a member of the Philippine Military Academy Class of 1986, was the first PNP chief of former president Rodrigo Duterte and chief implementor of his war on drugs. He is facing a warrant of arrest from the International Criminal Court as Duterte’s co-perpetrator in the crimes against humanity case for alleged atrocities in the past administration’s anti-drug campaign.
Police teams are searching for Dela Rosa, who has a P50-million bounty for his arrest that was put up by the Department of the Interior and Local Government.
Potential informants are calling the PNP’s hotlines for tips on Dela Rosa’s location, who is believed to be hiding somewhere in Mindanao, allegedly under the protection of an armed group.

Meanwhile, Sen. Panfilo Lacson has clarified his stance that a crimes against humanity fugitive like Dela Rosa also deserves due process, which includes bringing him before a domestic court before being taken to The Hague to face his cases.
Speaking to dzMM yesterday, Lacson said this would allow Dela Rosa to seek help before the Supreme Court so he could exhaust all available judicial relief before he could be surrendered.
Lacson said it would only be “ministerial” if Dela Rosa had to be brought before a local court. – Marc Jayson Cayabyab

articles.title: Witnesses vs Duterte to testify on DDS, killings
articles.summary: Several witnesses that the prosecution intends to present against former president Rodrigo Duterte in his crimes against humanity trial will focus on the killings committed by the so-called Davao…

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 12:00am

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on September 16, 2026, during a preparatory session as he faces charges over his “war on drugs,” which killed thousands.
AFP / Pool / Piroschka Van De Wouw

MANILA, Philippines — Several witnesses that the prosecution intends to present against former president Rodrigo Duterte in his crimes against humanity trial will focus on the killings committed by the so-called Davao death squad (DDS) and by the police during anti-drug operations.

International Criminal Court acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang recently filed three new requests for admission of the prior recorded testimonies of 10 witnesses that they intend to present against Duterte, in addition to the five earlier requests.

The sixth request, which covers witnesses P-1136, P-1345, P-1391 and P-1404, involved testimonies of “violence in the Philippines… prior to and during Mr. Duterte’s presidency.” Witness P-1136 specifically discussed the targeting of so-called high-value drug personalities, while witnesses P-1345 and P-1391 discussed details related to the drug war.
These included the targeting of alleged drug personalities, the use of drug watchlists and the supposed fabrication of accounts of killings committed by the Philippine National Police.
Accounts of witness P-1404 cover evidence related to barangay clearance operation.
The prosecution’s seventh request, which covers witnesses P-1097, P-1170 and P-1318, involves details related to the drug war’s implementation.
Witness P-1097 provides information on the implementation of Tokhang, which “involved killings rather than ‘knock and plead’ visits.”

Meanwhile, P-1170 would testify on the PNP’s role in the implementation of the drug war, while P-1318 would specifically allege that “some police killings were staged through nanlaban narratives, evidence planting and cover-ups.”
The eighth request, which covers witnesses P-0019, P-1032 and P-1409, involves testimonies of the DDS killings in the Davao area prior to Duterte’s election as president.

P-0019 will testify on extrajudicial killings in Davao City, including instances when Duterte – then either as mayor or vice mayor – read out names of criminal suspects, some of whom were subsequently killed.
Witness P-1032 will testify on the existence and the supposed composition of the DDS, as well as its operations targeting alleged criminals in Davao City.
Testimony of P-1409 will center on the existence of the DDS and its involvement in extrajudicial killings from 2016 to 2017, including financial rewards allegedly provided by Duterte to DDS handlers.
The prosecution alleged that the prior recorded testimonies of the witnesses were relevant to the case. Even if granted, they will still be presented in person for supplementary examination.
Niang argued that accepting their prior recorded testimonies will reduce the total time needed for their direct examination.
Duterte’s defense team will still be able to cross-examine them during trial.

articles.title: OSG to SC: Junk Padilla, Go petition
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court called on the Supreme Court to throw out the petition from two senators who challenged an earlier ruling to lower the voting threshold to convict Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court called on the Supreme Court (SC) to throw out the petition from two senators who challenged an earlier ruling to lower the voting threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.
The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) filed on Nov. 3 its comment on the petition for certiorari and prohibition filed by Sens. Robinhood Padilla and Bong Go, both Duterte allies.
According to the OSG, the Senate impeachment court wanted the SC to “dismiss the petition for certiorari and prohibition for being premature and for lack of merit.”
It wanted the high tribunal to “deny petitioners’ application for the issuance of a status quo ante order, temporary restraining order and writ of preliminary injunction.”
Padilla and Go wanted the SC to invalidate the Senate impeachment court's decision in September to lower the voting threshold based on the senators present at the trial.

From the 16 votes to convict, or two-thirds of all the 24 members of the Senate, the impeachment court’s decision lowered the count to a possible 14 votes since Sens. Jinggoy Estrada, Rodante Marcoleta, Ronald dela Rosa and Loren Legarda remain absent.

articles.title: Dizon eyes rider cap review
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon is eyeing a review of the cap on riders being enforced by the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board on motorcycle-taxi service providers, saying…

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 12:00am
Department of Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon.
STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines —Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon is eyeing a review of the cap on riders being enforced by the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) on motorcycle-taxi service providers, saying the current rule is no longer responsive to the needs of commuters and the industry.
“What I want to understand is what is the supply and demand situation of our public transport here in Metro Manila,” he told reporters.
“How many rides? How many riders are available? Because it is clear that there’s a scarcity,” he added.
Dizon said the current cap appears to be no longer applicable, given the surge in demand from commuters.
The development came after ride-hailing app Move It was fined P555.7 million by the LTFRB for exceeding the rider cap.
Rep. Rodge Gutierrez supports Dizon’s proposal to have the cap reviewed.
According to the LTFRB, Move It more than tripled its authorized limit of 17,746 rider-partners by 55,575 in Metro Manila, Cebu City, and Cagayan de Oro City.
Records showed that the company had 73,321 rider-partners.
The penalty for the offense is P10,000 fine per excess rider.

articles.title: Israel's president to begin consultations with parties after election deadlock
articles.summary: Herzog warned politicians that "not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled" if they want to avoid another election.

blocks.text: In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That makes them potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.

The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government. That person will be given 28 days to do so, with a potential 14-day extension.
The president has wide discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition. They do not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.
On Wednesday morning, Herzog was presented with the official results by Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg at a ceremony in Jerusalem.
"In recent days, we have heard voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy. This is a real danger," Sohlberg said.
"One of the foundations of democracy is the ability to have a peaceful transfer of power. This stems from the understanding that the will of the electorate obligates us all."
Herzog announced that he would begin the consultation process on Wednesday evening.

"In order to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable and good government here for the people of Israel, I expect the factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled," he said.
The president also expressed confidence in the Shin Bet's ability to investigate the allegations of foreign interference in the election and appealed for patience.
But he warned that Arab Israelis - who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel - "must not be smeared".
"I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them toward any community in Israel," he said.

Earlier, Sohlberg told a meeting of the Central Elections Committee that the Shin Bet's intelligence appeared to point to a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states", some of which were hostile.
It believed further investigation was needed to "connect the dots and determine the scale of the phenomenon with a high degree of certainty", he said.

Last week, Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's foreign ministry said it categorically denied the allegation.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party and an ally of the prime minister, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all the leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified".
Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and the prime minister of attempting to "steal the election from the public".
On Tuesday, Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and his Likud party were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law".

His comments came after Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini - an appointee of the prime minister - to interrogate four Arab politicians, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented.
Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying to "obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors".

articles.title: Spain’s deadly train crashes have damaged public confidence in the system
articles.summary:
Pedro Sánchez and his socialist-led coalition government are racing to rebuild trust ahead of a snap election, but the task they face is immense

•

blocks.text: A week ago today, for the second time in nine months, I got in my car and drove south from Madrid to cover a deadly train crash.

At 8.53am last Wednesday, a high-speed train operated by Spain’s state-owned rail company, Renfe, smashed into the back of a stationary train run by the private rail company Iryo, on the outskirts of the small town of Urda in Castilla-La Mancha. Sixty-nine people died in the accident, more than 100 were injured, and Spain’s already depleted confidence in its treasured rail network plummeted.

As I drove to Urda, I – along with much of Spain – was feeling a grim sense of deja vu. On 18 January, an Iryo train on the same line from Madrid to Seville had derailed near the Andalucían town of Adamuz before being struck by a Renfe train coming from the opposite direction. Forty-six people died, scores were injured and public trust in Spain’s trains was badly shaken.

The things I saw and heard in Urda mirrored those I’d seen and heard in Adamuz: local people rushing to the train tracks to help the injured; the rapid repurposing of municipal halls into emergency triage centres; and all manner of spontaneous acts of selflessness, bravery, practicality and compassion.

Some of the passengers whose journey south had come to a violent and premature end near Urda stood in line, many still with their wheelie cases and rucksacks, waiting for the coaches that had been chartered to take them onward. The queues looked almost normal until you noticed the odd bandaged head, torn trouser leg, or bloodstained top.

Josimar Medina, a young Peruvian who was travelling with his Brazilian girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, told me the blood on his brown T-shirt belonged to an American called Austin. Medina had helped free Austin from the wreckage and had managed to get him out of the train.

Although the young American was badly hurt, Medina had seen far worse injuries as he clambered off the train. “I saw … people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” he said. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”

The shock and sorrow has echoed around Spain as the country tries to come to terms with what has happened, and to accept that its extensive and modern speed rail system – long a source of national pride – may not be the safe and reliable network it once seemed.
As the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, put it last week, “public trust in the high-speed system has been broken”.
Sánchez and his socialist-led coalition government are now racing to rebuild that trust, but the task they face is immense – especially given the current circumstances.
How will this play out in the elections?

blocks.caption: Pedro Sánchez is leading a country in mourning. Photograph: GSLV/GTRES/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The anger and grief are still raw and, with a snap general election now less than a month away, the political atmosphere is explosive. The prime minister’s critics point out that 115 people died at Adamuz and Urda, and Sánchez and his ministers have had eight years to focus on, and invest in, rail safety. On Tuesday evening, the transport minister, Óscar Puente, accepted the inevitable, announcing his resignation, with the acknowledgment that “neither the country, nor I, can bear 100 deaths in less than a year”.
With the election drawing closer, the language from opposition parties is becoming more strident.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which is expected to finish first in next month’s vote, has accused the Sánchez administration of failing to keep Spaniards safe and of trying to use the latest tragedy to political ends.
after newsletter promotion
“It’s not just obvious that they’re not good at being in charge,” Feijóo said on Monday. “It’s that I’m also not sure that they’re good people, either.”

The far-right Vox party, with whom the PP could form a national coalition government, has been even more scathing, accusing the government of “killing” the train crash victims and of “incompetence, corruption, cronyism, and a lack of investment in maintenance and infrastructure improvements”. It is also urging the supreme court to investigate Puente on suspicion of manslaughter and causing bodily harm through gross negligence. Puente has rejected allegations of mismanagement, and has insisted that Spain’s railway system is “safe and reliable”.

Despite signs of a modest resurgence in support just before the latest crash, Sánchez always faced a tough road to re-election. Corruption scandals have bedevilled his inner circle and his government was much criticised for its response to the mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta over the summer. That road now looks even more impassable.

But with disasters, emergencies and deaths so frequently politicised, especially in Spain, the worry now is that solutions to the failings at Adamuz and Urda may be missed amid all the campaigning and point-scoring.
As the politicians bicker and Spain prepares for its fifth general election in 10 years, the long process of recovery is just beginning for some of those who survived last week’s crash.

On Saturday afternoon, I got an email from the family of Austin Hartman, the young American pulled out of the train by Josimar Medina. They told me that Austin, a Cal Poly State University student who had been studying in Madrid, was being treated in a Spanish hospital for multiple fractures to his pelvis, hip, femur, humerus and rib, and was unlikely to be well enough to return home for at least two months. GoFundMe pages have been set up for Austin and his friend Leah Silver-Fajardo, who was also badly hurt in the accident.

His family had seen the photo I took of Josimar and Vitoria in Urda and wanted to know if there was any way of contacting them so that Austin could say thank you. By the following day, Austin and his family had video called the couple.

“It was so helpful for us to … thank Josimar for treating Austin with such loving care when he needed it more than anything,” Austin’s stepmother, Sandi, told me in an email on Tuesday. “Austin credits him with saving his life. As we know, beautiful things are born of tragedy and it’s usually in the relationships that are formed out of it.”
To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday, please subscribe here.

articles.title: Gold for Palestine: Meet junior karate champ Mariam Bsharat
articles.summary: The occupied West Bank is not an obvious breeding ground for sporting success. But Mariam Bsharat, 17, has beaten the odds to become a karate world champion and is making a new life in Germany.

image.caption: Mariam Bsharat has won back to back world titles in karateImage: Fabienne Abu Wahib/Karate Insights/PS Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat said. "Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome."

Themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win. In Mariam Bsharat's case, it's about more than just dedication to training and taking care of the body. The 17-year-old won her second under-21 World Karate Championship gold medal competing for the Palestine national team in Poland in October.
"It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank.

"I faced challenges in transportation," Bsharat said. "I wasn't able to go from one city to another to be able to train with other people, so that I can actually prepare for competitions. I needed to travel to other countries like Jordan or Egypt ... which was very hard for me. And, financially, the support wasn't really the support an elite athlete needed."
Skepticism turns to sporting success
Growing up in Nablus, Bsharat had a narrow path to the top. But initially, it was her own reluctance that threatened to stop a champion career before it started.
"When I was a little kid, I did not really love it," said Bsharat, who competes in the division for fighters who weigh under 66 kilograms (145 pounds).

"I started it because my family was in that sport," Bsharat said. "My father had a dojo, and my mother also did that sport. My siblings and my aunts and my uncles — it's a family thing. I started it because they were all doing it. In time, I started getting into it."
How much power do Israeli settlers have over West Bank policy?

Family has been a constant source of comfort and inspiration for Bsharat. Her father and uncle have acted as manager and coach respectively. While her mother and siblings moved with Mariam to Hamburg, Germany, last year, her father remained in order to take care of his business, the dojo, though he visits and tries to be with his daughter in competitions. Integration has been made easier by her mastery of the language, taught to her by her German mother.
Bsharat has mixed feelings about leaving her homeland.

"I'm thankful to be here because being in Germany opened lot of doors for me, and I think I have a brighter future here," Bsharat said. "But also being in Palestine was just my everyday life, and I loved it there. My family was around me, my friends were around me, and I just felt comfortable, which was a big change coming here to Germany. I think every change comes with hardships."
Pressures from homeland weigh heavy

As well as the obvious difficulties of living in an area occupied by Israel, there are particular challenges for sportspeople living in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, with access to facilities, travel and constant security fears among them. As such, very few people from the Palestinian territories become successful on the international sporting stage. That, Bsharat said, gives her responsibilities that are unusual and heavy for a person of any age, let alone a 17-year-old.
Hamburg's refugee cricketers

"Being an elite athlete in Palestine is something very special because not everybody in Palestine has that opportunity. There aren't really a lot of athletes that are elite and who win international medals,” Bsharat said.

"So all that pressure from all the country and all the people, the family, the coaches are on me because I'm representing them, raising their flag,” she said. "I sometimes even forget to fight for myself and actually think about myself."
Olympic dream alive — should karate be an event again

That has not yet proved a barrier to Bsharat, who is is ranked first in the world in her category by the World Karate Federation (WKF). With Palestine recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Bsharat would likely have been a contender to raise that flag in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympics. But the sport was dropped from the Games in 2024.

"The global karate community remains steadfast in our belief that the natural place for karate is within the Olympic Games, and we sincerely hope that the incongruence we suffered in Paris 2024 and LA 2028 will be corrected for Brisbane 2032, if not sooner," the WKF wrote in response to the decision in 2024. The sport was also taken off the slate for the recent Youth Games in Senegal.

Should karate return in Brisbane, Bsharat would likely be approaching her prime. In the meantime, she is looking forward to starting her journey as a senior when she turns 18. But she won't be hanging around.
"My goal is it to be a world champion at seniors, which is the hardest and the best thing you can achieve in karate," she said.
"But winning an Olympic medal, being called Olympic champion or just representing my country with that flag [is a thought that] is just full of happiness and pride."
The interview was conducted by Janek Speight.

articles.title: Secret police files released in Hungary, 47 years after fall of communism
articles.summary: Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish.

blocks.text: Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule.
Critics say it has come too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members.
The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution.
"I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity," Prime Minister Péter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest.
"Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."

Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.

A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer.
Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.
These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided.
Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.
Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary.

Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.

Krisztian Ungváry, a historian who has long campaigned for the full release of the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power.

"In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna Borvendég, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party.
Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.
