articles.title: Menarco CEO Carmen Jimenez-Ong: Healthy homes should not be a luxury
articles.summary: In the Philippines, a housing shortage has forced many families to live in unsafe and high-risk areas.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 11:18pm
In the Philippines, a housing shortage has forced many families to live in unsafe and high-risk areas.
For years, around 50 families lived in cramped, makeshift homes inside an underground tunnel beneath Osmeña Highway in Manila before the government relocated them to Bulacan in September.
Meanwhile, around 1,000 families in Barangay Bagong Silangan, Quezon City, continue to live in a community without direct access to piped water and electricity.
Yet adequate housing is a human right, according to the United Nations Human Rights Office.
Housing, it says, is “a place to live in peace, security, and dignity.”
For Carmen Jimenez-Ong, founder and chief executive officer of award-winning real estate developer Menarco Development Corporation, access to healthy homes “is not a luxury.”
“It’s something that we should have as people,” she told GMA News in an interview on Wednesday. “It is very achievable.”

Jimenez-Ong said healthy homes are not necessarily about building more expensive houses but about building smarter. This includes ensuring adequate natural light, proper ventilation, and access to clean water, among other essentials.
“Creating a community within the space also makes it a healthy home,” she added.
She also emphasized the important role of the government in making healthy housing accessible.
“Government should provide that for the people. It is so basic,” she said.
Jimenez-Ong said Menarco is in talks with the national government and several local government units to gradually make healthy housing more accessible to Filipinos.
“We are being provided the opportunity to create healthy spaces for the people,” she added.
Menarco recently partnered with the Quezon City government to develop the Philippines' first WELL pre-certified socialized housing project in Barangay Old Balara.
Healthier communities
International WELL Building Institute head of Asia Pacific Jack Noonan said creating healthier spaces is crucial to building healthier communities.
“If we can build healthier buildings, we’re going to have healthier people, healthier communities, healthier societies… We’re building more resilient communities,” he said.
But healthy spaces should not be limited to homes. Workplaces also need to promote health and well-being, according to Noonan.

“If we’re able to create environments that promote health and well-being of the people who come to work in them, then we’re really helping the companies achieve greater success, because their people will become more productive and more happy being in the office,” NEO Office PH chief executive officer Raymond Rufino added.
“When the people are healthy, the country is healthy. It begins with the people,” Jimenez-Ong said. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Africa's shifting role in the global drug trade
articles.summary: Recent discoveries of meth labs suggest parts of Africa are moving beyond drug transit and becoming sites of synthetic drug production.
articles.byline: Isaac Mugabi, Adwoa Tenkoramaa Domena, Nontokozo Mchunu

image.caption: Once seen mainly as a transit route for drugs, parts of Africa are now emerging as production hubsImage: Olympia De Maismont/AFP

blocks.text: For years, Africa was primarily known as a transit point for international drug trafficking networks.
But recent drug seizures and laboratory discoveries show that illicit drugs are no longer only passing through African countries — they are increasingly being manufactured there.

Recent discoveries of methamphetamine laboratories in countries such as Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya and Mozambique have fueled concerns that Africa is becoming a significant production hub for synthetic drugs.

According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), synthetic drug production increasingly involves transnational criminal networks and clandestine laboratories capable of supplying both local and international markets.
Nigeria's biggest meth lab bust

The debate gained new urgency this year after Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) dismantled what the agency described as the largest clandestine methamphetamine laboratory ever uncovered in the country.

The operation in Nigeria's southwestern Ogun State led to the arrest of 10 suspects, including three Mexican nationals whom the NDLEA said had been brought into the country to help manufacture methamphetamine.
Nigerian authorities uncover largest meth lab

NDLEA's chairman, Mohamed Buba Marwa, said officers seized more than 2.4 metric tons of methamphetamine, precursor chemicals and other materials with an estimated international market value of about $363 million (€312 million).
The scale of the operation attracted widespread attention in Nigeria.

"It is no longer something you only see in movies," said DW correspondent Olisa Chukwumah. "The discovery raised serious questions about the level of local consumption if production is now happening in Nigeria."

Chukwumah said Nigerian authorities have uncovered meth laboratories before, but the size and sophistication of recent operations suggest that drug manufacturing networks are becoming more deeply established.
Why drug production is rising
Dokun Adedeji, co-founder of the Compassionate Care Recovery Initiative, said Nigeria's drug landscape has evolved significantly over the past decade.
"We used to think we were only a transit nation," he explained. "Then we became a consumer nation. Now we are discovering that we are also a production nation."
He noted that authorities have uncovered dozens of smaller laboratories over the years, with meth production sites identified in multiple states.
How drug cartels expand their reach across West Africa
According to the UNODC, increasing local drug consumption and the expansion of illicit drug markets have coincided with the growth of synthetic-drug production in West Africa.
The human cost of drugs
Adedeji described the impact of drug laboratories as "devastating and destructive."

He said substance abuse is contributing to school dropouts, family breakdowns, mental health challenges and rising criminal activity. Many families struggle to seek help because of stigma and fear of public judgment.
"We see families suffering every day," he said. "Many people are unable to speak openly about addiction because of concerns about reputation and discrimination."
The UNODC says young people are increasingly affected by drug-use disorders, with 34% of people receiving treatment for such disorders in Africa under the age of 25.

In addition to traditional drugs such as cannabis, users are increasingly turning to synthetic substances, including methamphetamine, often known on the streets as "ice." There is also growing misuse of prescription medications and reports of experimentation with dangerous inhalants and other toxic substances.
Can Nigeria curb drug production?
Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency has intensified enforcement efforts in recent years, leading to a series of high-profile drug seizures and arrests.
Nigeria faces synthetic marijuana drug crisis
NGOs have increasingly stepped in to fill the gap through awareness campaigns, particularly on university campuses where drug use is becoming more visible.
Chukwumah said there is still no coordinated, top-down policy approach and that much of the awareness work is being carried out by civil society groups.

Adedeji argues that policies based solely on punishment often drive users underground, making it harder for authorities and healthcare providers to identify and support people struggling with addiction.
UNODC and civil society groups advocate a broader response that extends beyond law enforcement.

Among the proposals being discussed are stronger national policies on substance abuse, expanded rehabilitation services, workplace drug prevention programs and increased regional cooperation across West Africa.
This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

articles.title: Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of new TV series' release
articles.summary: In 2001, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" hit cinemas and took the world by storm. Today, anticipation for the new series is high, but its creator, J.K. Rowling, remains a controversial figure.

image.caption: Rose to fame as Harry Potter: Daniel Radcliffe at the age of 12Image: Warner Bros/Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: On November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").
"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour."
The crowds showed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

blocks.caption: Emma Watson, Rupert Grint and Daniel Radcliffe in the 2001 filmImage: United Archives/IFTN/picture alliance

blocks.text: The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.
About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.
Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.
At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.
With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.
J.K. Rowling, a controversial author
For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.
But in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

blocks.caption: J.K. Rowling is one of the world's best-selling authorsImage: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.
Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.
The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

The "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.
Harry Potter TV series set to premiere at Christmas

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been announced, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.
The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

blocks.caption: The three actors in the series' lead roles: Arabella Stanton, Dominic McLaughlin and Alastair StoutImage: Aidan Monaghan/HBO/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the new production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump
articles.summary: From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. But can the Democrats now make…

image.caption: Soaring gas prices played a key role in the outcome of the midtermsImage: Patrick T. Fallon/AFP

blocks.text: For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one issue ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?
Market reaction: Is it all about AI and data centers?
Initial market reaction has been muted but trending negative. Global stocks fell slightly, while the dollar followed suit.

With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note.

"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind."

Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

blocks.caption: The Democrats will now control the US CongressImage: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, says the vote showed the extent of that opposition. Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

"This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he says. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted."

Brown points out that if the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.
What about Trump's tariff policies?

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms, particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats can force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

"Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office."

blocks.caption: Tariffs have been the signature economic policy of Trump's second termImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: While the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.
What about the war in Iran and surging oil prices?

Kirkegaard says that while Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.
Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.
Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall back, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.
"You've got to get a deal with Iran and you've got to bring down gas prices," says Kirkegaard. "From a political point of view, that's the most important thing now."

George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.
Could Democrat dominance force Trump to the table on the economy?
Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory across the board, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

Yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the new Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic issues to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," says Kirkegaard. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs."
Yet despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle trying to reverse them.
US midterms: Sweeping Democrat wins deliver rebuke to Trump

articles.title: B.C. mom delivers baby on side of highway while en route to Kamloops hospital
articles.summary: Marissa Ross was driving from Bridge Lake to Royal Inland Hospital in Kamloops to give birth to her fourth baby. But she didn't manage to make it to the hospital before her daughter made an…

image.caption: Marissa Ross delivered her fourth child, Remi, in the back of an ambulance along the side of Highway 24. She and her husband were on their way to Kamloops from Bridge Lake. (Submitted by Marissa Ross)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Marissa Ross was driving from Bridge Lake to Royal Inland Hospital in Kamloops to give birth to her fourth baby. But she didn't manage to make it to the hospital before her daughter made an appearance.
Marissa Ross had her 4th child while travelling to Kamloops from Bridge Lake
Marissa Ross never expected to be having her fourth child, a girl named Remi, on the side of the highway.
But that's exactly what happened when she went into labour last month.

Ross had a doctor's appointment in Kamloops on her due date, Oct. 20. She said her doctor thought she had a couple more days before she would give birth, so she returned to her home in Bridge Lake, about 140 kilometres northwest of Kamloops via Highway 24.
She arrived home and put her three other children to bed that night — then, she went into labour.
Ross and her husband Brandon packed up their brand new pickup truck — purchased weeks earlier to accommodate the growing family of six — and headed for Kamloops.
Marissa Ross says her nursing background helped her stay calm while delivering her child. (Submitted by Vanessa Mack)
Soon after, they realized they weren't going to make it to Royal Inland Hospital.
"My husband was driving and I said, you know what, I don't think we're going to make it to Kamloops," Ross said. "This baby's coming sooner.

"He's like, 'I'm calling an ambulance. You're not having this baby in the truck.' And so, before we lost cell service — because Highway 24 is not great for cell service — we quickly called [near] about [Lac des Roches]. And they said, 'We'll send somebody to meet you.'"
'Delivered the baby myself'
Ross was in the back of the pickup truck when the ambulance arrived.
The paramedic who assisted Ross was new and had not yet completed obstetrics training, according to Ross. He had called a specialist for help.
Ross, a registered nurse who works in post-natal care, took things into her own hands.
"I hopped onto the stretcher, and they did get me into the back of the ambulance, where I did push one more time and delivered the baby myself," she said.
"I was like, 'It's OK, calm down. I'm a nurse, I kind of know what I'm doing here,'" Ross added.

items: More stories from the B.C. Interior

blocks.text: Rare delivery
Vanessa Mack, the couple's birth and labour doula, says she got a call from the couple as they were leaving Bridge Lake and planned to meet them at the hospital.
She was surprised when she received a call soon after, saying the baby girl had arrived.
Mack says she has been to more than 100 births and this type of story is rare.
Baby Remi is doing well following her highway delivery, according to Ross. (Submitted by Vanessa Mack)

"What is cool about Marissa's story is she just kind of coached the ambulance attendants through the process, she coached the paramedics through her own birth," Mack said. "So really, I think all the power goes to her."
As for how the family is doing? They are settling into the chaos, and Ross's three boys are enjoying snuggles with their new baby sister.
"She's perfect," the mother said.

items: Video captures mom giving birth to daughter in a truck on Highway 407

blocks.text: In a statement, B.C. Emergency Health Services said ambulance and side-of-the-road deliveries are not unusual and that paramedics are trained to provide directions and assistance.
It said over the last year, paramedics assisted with the delivery of 67 babies in B.C.

articles.title: EU says Montenegro on track to become bloc's next member state by 2028
articles.summary: Brussels says Montenegro is likely to become the EU's 28th member state, followed by Albania and Moldova. It said Ukraine needed to speed up reforms and offered fresh hope to Serbia following…

image.caption: Montenegro is hoping to be the next member of the EU [FILE: Dec 16, 2024]Image: Martin Bertrand/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Union could finish accession negotiations with Montenegro as early as the end of the year, paving the way for the Balkan country to become the bloc's next member in 2028, the European Commission said Wednesday.

"This ​is testament to ​Montenegro's sustained efforts to advance on ​the European ‌path and implement the reforms needed ​to turn ⁠EU membership into reality," the EU's executive said in its annual enlargement policy report.
The EU said Montenegro was the frontrunner among nine candidate countries currently seeking membership. The last country to join the bloc was Croatia in 2013.

"The significant progress achieved by some candidates over the last year allows us to turn the promise of enlargement into reality," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. "Step by step, we are building a more complete, stronger Union."
EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028
What needs to happen for Montenegro to become an EU member?
The commission said Montenegro, with a population of 630,000, must still implement a number of reforms, particularly in the areas of fundamental rights and financial services.
If negotiations are wrapped up this year, an accession treaty could then be signed in June 2027, the report said.
The treaty would need to be ratified by all 27 EU member states, potentially allowing membership to be finalized in 2028.
As part of accession negotiations, candidate countries must bring their national laws and standards into line with EU requirements in areas ranging from environmental protection to human rights.
Montenegro has its sights on the EU
What is the status of other aspiring EU members?
The European Commission said in its report that Albania, Ukraine and Moldova were also making progress toward EU membership.

In its "roadmap" for the countries, it said Albania was roughly a year behind Montenegro and needed to continue reforming its justice system and tackling organized crime and corruption in order to finish accession negotiations by the end of 2027.
The commission said Moldova's aim of implementing the necessary reforms by early 2028 was also "ambitious but achievable" if the country continues to make changes at the current pace.

It praised Ukraine for making progress, despite the Russian invasion, but added that Kyiv needed to accelerate the pace of reforms to improve the rule of law and functioning of democratic institutions.
How far along is Serbia on the EU accession path?
Progress has been slower in the case of candidate countries North Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, the commission said.

But it also stressed that Serbia’s membership talks could get a boost if the student movement that beat longtime populist President Aleksandar Vucic last month forms a government willing to strengthen democracy.
"Now Serbia has the chance for a fresh start," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told EU lawmakers on Wednesday.

"The new Serbian government has an opportunity to turn the page, strengthen democratic institutions and fundamental rights, and take the necessary steps to advance on Serbia's accession path," she said.
Kosovo hopes to join the bloc but has not been granted candidate status.
Meanwhile, Georgia and Turkey are considered furthest away from attaining membership due to democratic backsliding.

articles.title: ICC may still hold confirmation of charges vs. Bato despite absence --counsel
articles.summary: The ICC could still hold its confirmation of charges against Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa despite his still being on the run, a lawyer for Duterte-era drug war victims said.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 9:56pm

The International Criminal Court (ICC) could still hold its confirmation of charges against Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa despite his still being on the run, a lawyer for Duterte-era drug war victims said.

In a 24 Oras report from Mariz Umali on Wednesday, ICC Assistant to Counsel Kristina Conti said that the tribunal could still hold a confirmation of charges hearing against Dela Rosa as an indirect co-perpetrator in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war.

“Pwedeng magkaroon kasi ng confirmation of charges hearing in the absence of the suspect. Nangyari yun last September lang, sa kaso ni Joseph Kony na hindi nila matukoy-tukoy kung nasaan, pero ang tagal na nakabinbin yung kaso. So, sa confirmation of charges hearing, posibleng absent yung akusado,” Conti said.

(There could be a confirmation of charges hearing in the absence of the suspect. That happened just in September, in the case of Joseph Kony, who cannot be found, but the case has been lodged for so long. So, in the confirmation of charges hearing, the accused could be absent.)
According to the Rome Statute, the confirmation of charges could be done against the accused if they could not be found or if they are trying to escape.
However, the accused must have a lawyer present to represent them, with the Pretrial Chamber Judges needing to approve of the matter as well.

This is what happened in September 2025 when the confirmation of charges were held against Kony, a Ugandan warlord. He faces 39 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity. The ICC had issued an arrest warrant against him in 2005 but he could not be found.

“Ang sabihin ng court, masyadong matagal na tayong naghihintay para sa paghuli nitong ganitong suspect. Kaya may hihiling dyan na pwede bang mag-proceed kami without the presence of the suspect,” Conti said.
(The court will say that we have been waiting too long for this suspect. So there is a plea to proceed without the presence of the suspect.)
Conti said that in the view of victims, these movements are still important and that it at least showed the case moving.

Dela Rosa has been on the run even before the ICC put out the arrest warrant for him in May. The senator was Duterte’s former police chief during the drug war, which saw the deaths of at least 6,000 people. — Jean Mangaluz/BM, GMA News

articles.title: Over 100 more dead pets found dumped in San Jose Del Monte, Bulacan
articles.summary: More than 100 additional dead pets have been found dumped at various locations across San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 9:56pm
More than 100 additional dead pets have been found dumped at various locations across San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.
In a "24 Oras" report from Bea Pinlac on Wednesday, pets were found in varying states of decay across the city. Some of the bodies were already riddled with worms.
“Most are too degraded and unidentifiable… we’re looking at probably around 120 bags or more,” said Chris Taylor, the founder of Luna and Furry Siblings Animal Welfare Rescue.
“One of the places that we suspect — they take from other vet clinics, other places, crematories that do not do their actual cremations. They contract out. So again, we’re not really sure,” he added.
The animal foundation is already working with the National Bureau of Investigation to retrieve the remains of the pets.

“This is on too large a scale. We're going to need the city, CENRO (City Environment and Natural Resources Office) and public health out here, because it’s just too massive and we’re going to need too many people to search the whole area, so really, it’s just going to be a manpower issue,” Taylor said.
This new dumping site was preceded by the initial site found in San Jose del Monte. The first dumping site was tied to a pet crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite.

“Titingnan yung composition; is it really yung ash coming from pets, animals or baka hindi… It will be up to the owners if they want to air their side… Kung wala naman po talaga siyang maling ginawa, face the music, give your side sa ating mga investigators… As of now, what we can see is possibly estafa plus civil damages,” Philippine National Police (PNP) spokesperson Col. Allen Rae Co said.

(We will see the composition; is it really ash coming from pets, animals, or maybe not… It will be up to the owners if they want to air their side… If they really did nothing wrong, face the music, give your side to our investigators… As of now, what we can see is possibly estafa plus civil damages.) —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Joy in Iran over ‘Trump’s defeat’ in US midterm elections – but war is not over
articles.summary: Iran celebrates its claimed role in ‘regime change’ amid pressure on US president to ‘finish the job’ with attack

blocks.text: Iran this week unveiled a massive new billboard and banners over Enqelab Square in central Tehran. The billboard pledged in English: “We will kill Trump” – elevating the degree of personal animus with which Donald Trump is viewed in official Iranian circles.

The poster depicts the US president behind bars with his head bowed. And in a sense, given the US midterm election results on Tuesday, Iran has indeed killed Trump, or at least the second term of his presidency. Trump’s reverse is all the more piquant because it comes on the day Iran’s leadership celebrates the anniversary of the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in 1979, an event that ensnared Jimmy Carter, and a reminder of how Iran has ruined the prospects of more than one US president.
Not surprisingly, the keenly followed election results have led to a good degree of triumphalism inside Iran.

Ehsan Movaheidian, an international relations scholar, claimed: “The Islamic Republic of Iran has succeeded in regime change in America. The same will soon happen in Europe as well. Bow down before the power of Iran.”

Meisam Zohurian, a conservative member of parliament, said: “The joy over the outcome of the US elections has nothing to do with the arrival of this party or the departure of that party. The issue is the aggressor was smeared in the dirt and Iran had an impact on the result.”
Ali Nikzad, the first deputy speaker of the parliament, said: “These electoral defeats are the aftershocks of Trump’s defeat by the Iranian people.”

blocks.caption: A student walks over Israeli and US flags during a rally on Wednesday marking the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the US embassy, outside the former embassy in Tehran. Photograph: Sobhan Farajvan/Pacific Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Iran’s supreme leader said anyone expecting a shift in US policy was “seriously mistaken”, however. “Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Mojtaba Khamenei wrote.
Others predicted further electoral defeats for what they considered to be the warmongers in Europe, and the expulsion of US bases from the entire Middle East.

The resistance – or bloody-mindedness – shown by Iran for the past eight gruelling months did allow the strait of Hormuz to become an Iranian-controlled channel through which inflation and high diesel prices were transmitted to the American system. Even Trump himself on Wednesday accepted, and lamented, that the American people had decided the “short-term” pain of inflation was not a price worth paying to prevent Iran becoming a nuclear power.

But the big question now is whether either side will regard these seismic results as a moment to review their diplomatic strategy. Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, was quick to call on Trump to accept the wisdom of the American people. On social media he urged Trump to bow to the verdict of America: “Whether driven by conscience or the cost of living, America said no to war and we endorse this message.”
Ghalibaf added: “If the US government betrays the public will in order to serve international paymasters and blackmailers it will learn our ‘no’ comes with a nightmare.”

Yet Iran will also be asked to reflect on the wisdom of war by the Gulf monarchies, and possibly by Russia and China – the latter a country that seems finally to be stirring itself to find a solution to the blockade in the strait of Hormuz that is preventing badly-needed Middle East oil exports from reaching its industries.

China tends to knock only on doors that it knows are going to open, so it is probably testing the feasibility of a deal in which Iran “downblends” – or dilutes – its stockpile of highly enriched uranium inside Iran under international supervision. A Chinese special envoy is travelling to Oman, Iran and Saudi Arabia almost immediately.

These countries, some sympathetic to Iran’s predicament, can point out that if Tehran ever thought in the run-up to the elections Trump would capitulate and turn his carrier fleet around, it was mistaken. Some Iranian diplomats had indeed hoped that the prospect of defeat in the midterms, and pressure from within the Republican party, would have led Trump to make concessions to Tehran.
after newsletter promotion

In fact, both sides and the chief mediator, Qatar, clearly did try to use polling day as a lever, but in the end neither side retreated. Trump, for once, was true to his word and refused to allow the darkening opinion polls to reduce his determination to keep Iran in his vice. Confined to a holding bay of “neither war nor peace”, Trump’s priority was to keep the oil price as low as possible by repeatedly suggesting a settlement might be imminent.

For the next two months before the new Congress convenes in January – so reducing his budgetary options – Trump has greater latitude, and little accountability. The damage to the Republican party has been done and cannot be undone.

Unsurprisingly the Trump influencers who advocated for the war in the first place are piling on pressure to strike again quickly. Laura Loomer wrote on X: “Time for President Trump to deal with Iran once and for all. Just do it, Nothing to lose now. Finish the job.”

But the credibility of Loomer and her like has been severely damaged: in February, she had advised Trump that regime change in Iran – “a little excursion” – could be as easy as knocking over the Maduro regime in Venezuela. Similarly, Benjamin Netanyahu is now touting intelligence showing that Iran is preparing to use chemical weapons. The ease with which the Israeli prime minister conjures up intelligence to justify another assault on Iran may by now have struck the White House.

Hillary Clinton, Trump’s old sparring partner, is one who thinks Trump will probably launch the long-delayed attack. She said: “I think he will feel trapped. He will feel angry and resentful and he will react aggressively.”

Having come so far, and paid so high a political price, Trump may in the next two months try to secure a legacy by finishing the job – however he defines that. He is convinced, as he told Fox News this week, that “Iran has very few missiles and drones left, and even less capacity to build any more”. He crowed: “We are dealing with total strength. We can end it any time.”
Unfortunately, such blithe optimism has been heard before.

articles.title: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
articles.summary: Some Republicans tell the BBC the president's focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost them.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The result amounted to a rejection of Trump, one top Republican lobbyist said
ByDaniel Bush
Washington correspondent
Inside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.

After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress.

"It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."
Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power.
But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington.
"It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."
A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November.
"There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".

items: FOLLOW LIVE: Election results and analysis of the US midterms
Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland
Key moments from a night of midterm election firsts
Five reasons why Trump did so badly

blocks.text: The BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.

Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.
But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda.
The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results

"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".
Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats.
"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.

He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Republican Senator Jon Husted at an election event in Ohio, where the Senate seat flipped in favour of Democrat Sherrod Brown

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Republican Senator Jon Husted at an election event in Ohio, where the Senate seat flipped in favour of Democrat Sherrod Brown

Since 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.

Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.

Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.

Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.

Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."
Others defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel.

"He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.
That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.

Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina.
"That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Republican supporters at a watch party in Iowa, where Democrat candidate Josh Turek won a Senate seat

blocks.text: Republican supporters at a watch party in Iowa, where Democrat candidate Josh Turek won a Senate seat
Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election.

Trump was consumed by the war with Iran abroad and his construction overhaul of Washington at home. The projects included the under-construction ballroom and a helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, renovations to a local golf course, a proposed memorial arch near Arlington Cemetery and renovations to the Kennedy Center.

Events like a UFC match at the White House on Trump's 80th birthday in June created the impression that the president was more interested in feting himself than winning the midterms, several sources said. Trump also repeatedly downplayed the rising costs of gas and often cast the affordability issue as a Democratic hoax.

Trump turned his full attention to the election in September at the Republican Party's midterm convention. The event was a gamble: Republicans hadn't held a midterm convention in decades, and it was an open question whether voters would tune in.
Trump dominated the convention in Dallas, frustrating Republicans who told the BBC they wanted to highlight the party's midterm candidates.

In his rambling keynote speech, Trump pledged to give $5,000 (£3,700) to anyone who voted for Republicans and raised eyebrows with an endorsement of Paxton which included a lengthy criticism of the candidate's lack of charisma and physical appearance.

"Obviously, that's never helpful," Robin Armstrong, Texas' Republican National Committeeman, said of Trump's critique of Paxton. "You're not going to stop what President Trump says. We just have to kind of live with that."

The convention failed to attract a large television audience, and Democrats were quick to call it a failure. "It backfired for Republicans because nobody paid any attention to it," said Terri Burke, the Texas Democratic Party's executive director.

Trump's penchant for straying off-message continued when he hit the campaign trail in the final weeks before Election Day. He made headlines for praising Ohio Republican Senator John Husted's physique, and drew criticism for calling El-Sayed a "jihadist" in the Michigan Senate race.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mike Rogers in Michigan was among the other losing candidates - having been beaten to a Senate seat by Democrat Abdul El-Sayed

blocks.text: Mike Rogers in Michigan was among the other losing candidates - having been beaten to a Senate seat by Democrat Abdul El-Sayed

As Trump criss-crossed the country stumping for Republican candidates, the White House contended with controversies in Washington. Katie Zacharia was ousted after just five days as White House press secretary, and Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the US ambassador to Greece after reports surfaced that she asked a donor to pay her credit card debt.

Trump also faced a backlash in October for striking a deal to buy Russian diesel. The agreement, which blindsided members of Congress and drew condemnation from some Republicans, came just weeks after Trump signed a sanctions bill aimed at cutting off Russian oil and gas revenue.

Democrats used the deal and other scandals swirling around the White House to make the case for retaking control of Congress. The messaging resonated in the end, as Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress in convincing fashion.
A second White House ally said that the president's political aides projected optimism until the final days of the election, even as it became clear the party was headed to defeat.
Now, as Republicans take stock of the loss, several said they were ready to look ahead to the 2028 election.
"Whether that's JD Vance, or Macro Rubio, or Ted Cruz, we've got a pretty big bench," said Scheffler, the state's RNC member. "It'll be a wide open race."

Peppin, the Republican strategist, said the midterms results demonstrated the party needed a new direction. "I sincerely hope that we've turned the page from the Trump era, and that we'll have new players, new issues and a new focus moving forward."

articles.title: Leading ice hockey nations, sponsors oppose Russia's return
articles.summary: Ice hockey's governing body says the impact of a court decision forcing it to reinstate Russia presents "significant practical and sporting challenges." Several leading nations say they won't play…

image.caption: The Court of Arbitration says Russian teams can return to international ice hockey, but against whom? And where?Image: Maksim Konstantinov/Imago Images

blocks.text: The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated."

It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward."

Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS said that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence."

Wednesday's statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.

Two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month, and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.
'Russians will not be in Canada'
On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

blocks.caption: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has ruled out Russian participation in the World Junior Ice Hockey Tournament in Alberta next monthImage: Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship."
Lutz was to discuss the matter with government officials in Berlin this week. A government spokesman said on the weekend that Berlin "takes a very critical view" of the ruling.
Growing European boycott of Russia
Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland, the defending men's world champions, has been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.
"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.
Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.
"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said.
This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.
Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.
Latvia's federation said it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.
Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia."
USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.

blocks.caption: The AJ Products and Skoda logos have long been a familiar sight at World Ice Hockey ChampionshipsImage: Richard Wareham/IMAGO

blocks.text: Sponsors having second thoughts

At the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades, told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.

"We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker said.

Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.

With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.

articles.title: Nadal set to join Real Madrid board of directors
articles.summary: Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.

blocks.text: Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.
Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and helped Spain claim five Davis Cups before retiring in 2024.
Real's members will be asked to approve the 40-year-old's appointment to the board at a meeting later this month.
In a statement announcing the move, external, the club said Nadal was "one of the greatest legends in the history of sport and one of the most admired and recognised Spanish athletes in the world".

"It is a great source of pride that a figure of his sporting and human stature, a benchmark of Spanish and world sport, will become part of our board of directors and contribute, from this position of responsibility, to the present and future of our club," Real added.
The tennis legend - a boyhood Real fan who holds member's number 67,778 - included a photo of himself as a child in a club kit in his response to the news.
"I want to thank president Florentino Perez and the board for proposing that I join the board of directors of Real Madrid," Nadal said in his post on X, external.
"I have accepted this proposal with great excitement, a desire to learn, and a willingness to contribute everything I can."
It is currently unclear as to what responsibilities Nadal would hold on the club's board.
Perez was re-elected to serve a new four-year term as Real president in June, having held the office since 2009.

He swiftly appointed Jose Mourinho to a second spell as head coach, hoping to improve the club's fortunes after they went a second season without a trophy in La Liga, the Champions League or the Copa del Rey.
Real are currently third in the league after 11 games - three points behind defending champions Barcelona.

articles.summary: Democrats flip seven Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Maine, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina; ‘blue wave’ rejects Trump’s agenda

blocks.text: Democrats secure majority in the House as voters punish Republican Party
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

In case you fell asleep early, yesterday evening resonated as an extinction level-event for Donald Trump’s Republican Party, a worst-case scenario for the GOP that even the starkest polls might’ve underestimated.

Democrats defended a crucial Senate seat in Michigan and won the likely pickups in Maine and North Carolina. They then proceeded to flip five more seats in states that would normally be considered unquestionably red: Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina, and — the biggest prize of them all — Texas.

As of Wednesday morning, Democrats have secured 54 seats in the Senate. A closely-watched race in Alaska is yet to be called. And the Senate contest in ruby red Mississippi is down to the wire, with Democrat Scott Colom leading by just a few dozen votes as the final ballots roll in.

The Democrats have already secured 228 seats in the House, ten more than needed for a majority, and could realistically run up the score to 240 seats or more. They’ve also flipped governor’s offices in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Nevada.
Republicans, needless to say, are shell-shocked, with the future of the party deeply uncertain, and some sounding the death-knell for a decade of Trump-dominated GOP politics.
Here are some other developments you may have missed last night:

items: Trump, uncharacteristically gracious, accepted his party’s resounding defeat, congratulated Democrats, and told The New York Times that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the election results. That was very much in doubt after the Trump administration spent months seeking to exert greater influence over the elections process through executive orders and the courts.

Deb Haaland, running in New Mexico, became the first Native American woman elected as governor. Keisha Lanca Bottoms became the first Black woman ever elected governor. Abdul El-Sayed, the victorious Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, became the first Muslim voted into the upper chamber.
Several key congressional races, including contests in Colorado, Michigan, Maine, New York, California, and North Carolina, remain to be called.

articles.title: Indonesia deploys troops to Jakarta after wiretapping allegations
articles.summary: Indonesian troops are being stationed in Jakarta amid wiretapping allegations implicating the president's chief of staff. Suspects are being accused of illegally tapping the president's phones.

image.caption: President Prabowo Subianto's government has yet to determine the motiveImage: BPMI Setpres/Kris

blocks.text: Indonesia's military deployed more than 20,000 troops and personnel to the capital city Jakarta after authorities launched an investigation into an alleged wiretapping operation targeting the President Prabowo Subianto.
Some 20,000 troops have been deployed in Jakarta amid the scandal with the president's chief of staff is currently being investigated.
Senior military figures implicated
So far, three senior police generals have been detained. They are being accused of illegally tapping the phones of the president, journalists, politicians and business people.
Among those detained is Listyo Sigit Prabowo — not related to the president — who was the national police chief before becoming the president's chief of staff last month.
The presidential palace claims the alleged wiretapping targeting President Subianto could be regarded as an act "tending towards treason."
The authorities did not officially confirm that the deployment is connected to the scandal.
The number of troops and personnel deployed to the capital since Monday surpassed 20,000 as of Wednesday, according to the navy operations assistant, Vice Admiral Yayan Sofiyan.
Indonesian armed forces spokesperson Major General Muhammad Nas claimed that the troop movement was a "standart procedure" for maintaining national security.
Motive yet to be established
According to Indonesia's senior minister for legal affairs, the government has yet to determine the motive for the wiretapping.
The suspects, who have not responded publicly to the allegations, could face unlawful surveillance related charges, which can lead up to 10 years in prison.

"There is a strong suspicion that the wiretapping was carried out not in the interests of the state or the National Police, but for the interests of other parties,” Adrianus Meliala, a criminologist at the University of Indonesia and a former commissioner of the National Police Commission said.

"No one expected Listyo Sigit Prabowo to be named a suspect,” said Meliala, "But if the allegations are proven, the case could be understood in the context of political maneuvering. Anyone who engages in politics must also be prepared to face the political consequences," Meliala said.

articles.title: Hungary opens communist-era secret police files identifying informants
articles.summary: The archives name thousands of former informants who spied on citizens for the state security services during decades of one-party rule. The prime minister said "many families will now face difficult…

image.caption: Prime Minister Peter Magyar (right) announced the release of records at the headquarters of the state security archivesImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: Hungary released thousands of communist-era secret police records to the public on Wednesday as part of the country's long-delayed effort to come to terms with its repressive past.

The archives, which are now part of a searchable online database, include the names of thousands of former informants who worked for the state security apparatus during four decades of one-party rule.
Although communism ended in Hungary in 1989, attempts to open the files had been repeatedly stalled. Some critics blamed the delay on successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures.
Historic move 36 years after transition to democracy
Center-right Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who unseated longtime populist leader Viktor Orban in April, had pledged to grant the public unrestricted access to the records.

"After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives on Wednesday.
He said ​some 60,000 ‌names had been made public in the new online database. A second batch of files is expected to be made available by February.

"I ask ‌everyone ​to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity ... as many families will now face difficult information often related to a deceased member of their family," Magyar said. "​It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."
Coming to terms with totalitarian past
Hungary was under one-party communist rule from 1949 to 1989.

As was the case in a number of Eastern European countries during the Cold War, secret police in Hungary relied on a vast network of informants to monitor citizens. These informants were often coerced into reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives.
According to estimates from the state security archives, authorities recruited some 150,000 informants, although records for about two-thirds of them no longer exist.
Many files were destroyed in 1956 during Hungary's anti-Soviet uprising, or hidden during the transition to democracy. Some are believed to have been taken to Moscow.

blocks.caption: Many of the files are thought to have been destroyed during the 1956 anti-Soviet uprising Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Better late than never'
Historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation told the AFP news agency that the move to make the files public was "better late than never."
"We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.
He predicted the release would trigger public and private revelations, saying it "could cause some hysteria in the coming months."
Ahead of the publication, rumors had circulated that Former Prime Minister Orban was an informant, but his name did not appear in the digital database on Wednesday.
Orban said on Tuesday that communist secret services had tried to recruit him while he was doing his military service, but he refused.

articles.title: PH Police find child abuse imagery on devices tied to Thomas Markle
articles.summary: Philippine police told AFP on Wednesday that three memory cards and a cell phone turned over by the son of Meghan Markle's estranged father contained child sexual abuse material.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 8:35pm
Philippine police told AFP on Wednesday that three memory cards and a cell phone turned over by the son of Meghan Markle's estranged father contained child sexual abuse material.

Last week, Philippine police said they were investigating a laptop found alongside images of child abuse at an alleged former residence of Thomas Markle, whose daughter is married to Britain's Prince Harry.
Philippine interior minister Jonvic Remulla told AFP at the time the country planned to take "appropriate legal actions" if sufficient evidence was found. Markle has denied all claims against him.
On Wednesday, the country's national police said child abuse materials had been discovered among the cache turned over by Markle's son amid an "intensifying" investigation.

"It is not enough to simply come across some materials and immediately draw conclusions," Philippine national police chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said, in a statement provided in response to questions about the investigation.
"We have to establish where these came from, who may be responsible, and whether Philippine laws were violated," he said.
The revelation came a day after Mexican authorities raided a storage unit rented by Thomas Markle as part of the ongoing investigation.
The prosecutor's office of Mexico's Baja California state said Monday it had received an anonymous tip about the existence of child sex abuse material in a storage unit rented by Thomas Markle.
Investigators said the owner of the storage unit reported Markle had stopped paying rent for it in 2024 but his possessions remained secured inside.
Authorities reported finding "magazines from Asia" dating back 20 years, without giving further details, as well as computer equipment that has been taken in for further investigation.
British tabloid The Sun first reported last month that Markle's son, Thomas Markle Jr, had discovered the child abuse images while going through boxes found in his father's former home.
Markle had been living in Cebu in the Philippines until reportedly returning to the United States earlier this year.

Meghan Markle has previously said she was "deeply distressed" by accusations that her father had possessed images of child abuse, adding she had blocked contact between him and her children over previous "troubling and disturbing" allegations. — Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Sharp objects found in Halloween sweets in three European nations
articles.summary: Dozens of cases are reported in Austria, Germany and Hungary, including a nine-year-old girl hurting her tongue while eating chocolate containing a pin.

blocks.text: Needles and other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets handed out over Halloween in Germany, Austria and Hungary, prompting police to issue warnings to parents to check what their children have been given.
Police in a number of German states have reported cases, from Bavaria in the south-east to Lower Saxony in the north.
A girl aged nine hurt her tongue while eating a chocolate bar in Bremervörde, west of Hamburg. A 5cm-long (2in) pin was then found inside it.

Meanwhile, police in Hungary have launched a criminal investigation after nails, screws and pieces of wire were found in sweets handed out to children who had been trick-or-treating in and around the town of Gyömrő, to the east of Budapest.
The local authority said one young girl had been handed a toffee with a nail inside a chocolate wrapper and that she had fortunately noticed in time and had not swallowed the sweet.
Several cases have also been reported across Austria, where Interior Minister Gerhard Karner condemned the incidents as "cowardly, malicious and in some cases life-threatening".

articles.title: Israel’s election commission rejects Netanyahu claims of voting fraud
articles.summary:
Move comes after attorney general blocked Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties

Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of the…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of the 27 October vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of their governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.

His main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, warned that Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy”, attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Hours earlier Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties, because she was not presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.

“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.

blocks.caption: People take part in a rally in Tel Aviv calling for the opposition to form a government with the Arab parties after last week’s general election. Photograph: Jamal Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: “The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, added that some “suspicions” were still under investigation, but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over Herzog also denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens, who turned out to vote at historic rates.

“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”

Herzog plays a key role in formation of the next government, by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, in an announcement that could come as early as Thursday evening.

A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Palestinian-led parties have said their priority is removing Netanyahu so are also expected to back him as the strongest contender to achieve that.

However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He also accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in a bid to hold on to power.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot has secured the public support of all the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Photograph: Paulina Patimer/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement, and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.

The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would allow harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Analyst Nadav Eyal warned that Israelis should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel,”

Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel, about 20% of the population, and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.

Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as the news of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.

“(The) Attorney General is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”
