articles.title: A nuclear Philippines in six years? OECD’s nuclear chief isn’t convinced.
articles.summary: The head of the OECD's Nuclear Energy Agency casts doubt on the Philippines' 2032 nuclear target, saying that getting its first reactor operating will likely take longer than six years

blocks.text: The head of the OECD's Nuclear Energy Agency casts doubt on the Philippines' 2032 nuclear target, saying that getting its first reactor operating will likely take longer than six years

items: The OECD-NEA director-general stated that the Philippines is unlikely to have its first nuclear reactor operational by 2032, citing the lengthy development process and the nascent regulatory environment.
The Department of Energy's draft guidelines suggest initial electricity deliveries from nuclear projects may start in 2038, six years later than the government's original target.
Public support for nuclear energy in the Philippines is relatively high, but concerns about nuclear waste management and community acceptance remain significant challenges.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines is unlikely to have its first nuclear reactor operating by 2032, according to the head of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Nuclear Energy Agency (OECD-NEA), who warned that developing a nuclear power plant would take longer than six years.

“I don’t think you’re going to have the first reactor operating in six years. It simply takes longer than that. You might have a decision in six years,” OECD-NEA director-general William Magwood told reporters on Wednesday, November 4.

“There’s a lot of discussions that have to be had between governments, between the utility and vendors. These take years to go through,” he added. “And the regulator is still very nascent. It’s just getting started. So no, it won’t happen in five or six years. But it will certainly happen within the foreseeable future if things stay on track.”

The international nuclear expert’s assessment comes less than a month after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed that the government’s target of introducing 1,200 megawatts (MW) of nuclear capacity by 2032 was achievable.

That timeline is already being reconsidered by Energy Secretary Sharon Garin. In addition, the Department of Energy’s (DOE) draft nuclear power capacity tender guidelines is already framed more conservatively, with initial electricity deliveries in 2038, six years later than Marcos’ endorsed target. This timetable applies to projects under the proposed tender though, meaning earlier projects through other arrangements may also be possible.

blocks.caption: TIMELINE. DOE’s timeline in its draft nuclear capacity tender as of September 2026 shows a first target delivery date of 2038.

blocks.text: “The draft nuclear energy tender does indicate already that delivery starts in 2038. And we’ve also gone on record in statements that we will stick to what’s in the plan,” DOE Director IV Patrick Aquino told reporters. “As you know, nuclear power projects takes a long time, takes a lot of push, so we are still not officially changing. We’re still hopeful on getting it done.”

With the ambitious goal, the DOE has been busy hosting forums and courting nuclear experts, suppliers, and developers. However, some early roadblocks have already appeared, with the Philippine Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (PhilATOM) still awaiting the appointment of its leadership and its unfinished implementing rules and regulation.

Beyond setting up the regulator, Aquino said the DOE was pursuing capacity-building initiatives, including human resource development and technical cooperation with countries that already operate nuclear facilities.

Magwood, however, warned that recruiting qualified personnel remains a “very big struggle” even in OECD countries, with nuclear regulators requiring specialists in engineering, science, geology, and other fields.

blocks.caption: Filipinos helped build UAE’s nuclear plant. PH talent may soon do the same back home.

blocks.text: Then there is the issue of getting the public to accept nuclear energy, with its risks and long-lasting waste.
So far, DOE surveys have shown relatively strong nationwide support for nuclear energy, with approval rising from 79% in 2019 to 82% in 2024.

Aquino said acceptance in communities being considered for nuclear development has also been relatively high, ranging from 60% to 90% depending on the location. Potential sites assessed include Bataan, Palawan, Masbate, Pangasinan, and Camarines Norte, while another nationwide survey is being prepared.
Still, Magwood cautioned that support could vary between communities.

“People in Philippines seem to be ready to have this conversation and to see where it takes them,” he said. “There’s a lot of support in some parts of the country and in other parts, maybe not as much. That’s pretty typical.”
Among the concerns is nuclear waste, which can remain dangerously radioactive long after it is removed from a reactor.

Magwood said there already exists technology to safely store spent nuclear fuel in specialized containers for decades before eventual disposal in geological repositories. However, he acknowledged that despite the technological advances made, nuclear waste is still “a very emotional topic,” especially for host communities.
While expressing confidence that the Philippines could manage nuclear waste, Magwood acknowledged that the country has yet to determine its approach to final disposal.
“The cost comes at the final disposal. But the Philippines hasn’t decided on that yet so it’s hard to put a cost estimate to it,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: More than 1,000 alleged communist terrorist group members have been neutralized so far in military operations this year, the NTF-ELCAC said.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 7:52pm
More than 1,000 communist terrorist group members have been neutralized so far in military operations this year, the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) said.

In a statement, the task force said that 1,355 alleged communist terrorist group members have been neutralized. Of this number, 1,227 surrendered, 48 were arrested, and 79 were killed during military operations.
The NTF-ELCAC also asked member agencies to prioritize programs that would help the reintegration of former rebels.

NTF-ELCAC Executive Director Danilo Pamonag said that a total of 27,897 former members and supporters of the Communist Party of the Philippines, New People’s Army, and National Democratic Font have returned to the society since 2022.

Pamonag also urged the Armed Forces of the Philippines, the Philippine National Police, the National Intelligence Coordinating Agency, the Department of Information and Communications Technology, and National Bureau of Investigation, “to track, flag and integrate cybersecurity measures to address online radicalization and terrorism financing schemes.”
Moreover, the amnesty board is also facilitating the processing on 13,841 amnesty applications of former rebels.

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. granted amnesty to rebel groups in 2023 through Proclamation Nos. 403, 404, 405, and 406, covering the CPP-NPA-NDF, MNLF, MILF, and the RPMP-RPA-ABB. The scope of amnesty varies per group. — Vince Angelo Ferreras/BM, GMA News

articles.title: DA admits submitting wrong coordinates for 8 proposed 2027 farm-to-market roads
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) on Wednesday admitted that eight farm-to-market road (FMR) projects included in its proposed 2027 budget contained incorrect coordinates due to encoding and…

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 7:38pm

The Department of Agriculture (DA) on Wednesday admitted that eight farm-to-market road (FMR) projects included in its proposed 2027 budget contained incorrect coordinates due to supposed "encoding and geotagging errors."
DA Assistant Secretary for Operations U-Nichols Manalo disclosed this during a hearing of the House agriculture and food committee on the government's response to El Niño.
Manalo said the eight projects were among the 1,669 FMR projects nationwide included in the DA's proposed budget under the National Expenditure Program (NEP).

“We’d like to inform the committee that the 1,669 farm-to-market road projects are within the NEP (National Expenditure Program) [proposed to the House]. Hindi iyon dun sa sinasabi nating inserted farm-to-market road projects,” Manalo said.
(These 1,669 FMR projects were not among those inserted by lawmakers.)

Manalo made the clarification after budget watchdog People’s Budget Coalition flagged provisions in the proposed 2027 national budget, which the House had approved on third and final reading, over allegedly incorrect project coordinates.
The group earlier cited hundreds of farm-to-market road (FMR) projects, questioning their locations and the transparency of the project allocations.
The group reported that some projects had coordinates pointing to bodies of water, including the Celebes Sea and the Philippine Rise.
Manalo attributed the errors in the eight FMR projects to “encoding and geotagging errors.”
Camarines Sur 4th District Rep. Arnie Fuentebella urged the DA to acknowledge and correct the errors while the proposed national budget was still under deliberation in the Senate.
“I think you can still correct it,” Fuentebella said.
“We appreciate you acknowledging your mistake,” he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Wawira Njiru, Kenya's school feeder and German Africa Prize recipient
articles.summary: From a small fundraiser to a major enterprise, Wawira Njiru's Kenyan school feeding scheme has been more successful than she ever thought possible. She's now being awarded the German Africa Prize.

image.caption: Wawira Njiru, founder and CEO of Food4Education, receives the 2026 German Africa PrizeImage: Food4Education

blocks.text: From starting a modest fundraiser for 25 school children, Wawira Njiru, 35, has become a social entrepreneur with a staggering 6,000 staff on her payroll, feeding 600,000 kids in Kenya every day with her organization Food4Education (F4E), an engagement for which she is being honored with this year's German Africa Prize. How did this transformation come to pass?
The answer may be in her character. Stubborn and hardworking, that's how Njiru sees herself. "It's hard to tell me something is not possible."

Thinking back to how she began, she explained, "My dream then, my ambition was to feed 100 kids every day. I was 21 years old then, so also having an ambition of feeding 100 kids felt momentous. But now growing up, but also figuring out that you can do more, and just being obsessed with 'How much more can you do? How much more can you do?' led me here."
Njiru left her native Kenya after finishing school to study nutrition science in Adelaide, Australia.
Feeding young minds: Wawira Njiru’s mission to keep children learning
Connecting the dots
"I knew a lot of kids back home were not getting the education they needed. At that time, I was learning about the impact of food, and I didn't realize how powerful food was," Njiru said.
"When you're doing a nutrition degree, that's when you really learn about the science behind food. And knowing that, especially for kids, it's so critical that they get nutritious meals."
When she found out her friends at the university often had a few dollars to spare and were looking for ways to contribute, she connected the dots and started her first fundraiser.
From there, the trajectory was set. But the road was rough at times for the young woman she was, Wawira explained. Some people didn't take her seriously. Others did.
"You have to find your believers," Njiru found out. "You can't just go with your own name. You have to find someone to vouch for you or someone or something to validate your presence."
Her degree certainly helped. But still, many men looking for jobs just didn't seem confident in working for a young woman. This is why more than 70% of her employees today are women, Njiru said.
School meals at 3 cents, digitally tracked

Steadily pushing the limits, Food4Education now provides 19,000 schools across Kenya with more than 600,000 meals every day. The system relies on a mix of funding: through donations and government funding, parents are left with a small contribution, which in some cases amounts to 5 Kenyan shillings (3 US cents).

Payment is processed through the so-called "Tap-to-Eat" system. Every child has a wristband that is used to track each meal. The wristbands not only track parents' payments, but they also help document how many meals are actually served. And if children don't pick up their meals, the team can find out why.

The model also relies on local sources wherever possible. About 80% of the food the organization distributes comes from small-scale farmers. This way, school meals are freshly sourced — and farmers have a reliable market for selling their produce.
How Kenya is fighting hunger in schools
"For a long time, school meals were viewed as charity. We've proven that it's economic infrastructure," Njiru said.
Boosting attention and morale among school children
Does it pay out? It seems so. Data show that children at participating schools miss fewer classes, and they also perform better at school.
"Food is everything," said Raphaera Kanya, director of a primary school in Kenya's capital Nairobi. "When your stomach has nothing, you cannot understand anything in class."
To Jane Nyambura, a pupil, the school feeding fosters equality at school.
"There was a difference because there are some students who are finding accessing food very easy because their parents are available," she told DW.
"There are others who can't afford food, and they feel as if it's unfair, as if there's something lacking in them. So it really demoralizes them and reduces their confidence."

blocks.caption: It's easier to concentrate and learn when you're well-fedImage: Andrew Wasike/DW

blocks.text: Njiru has already set her sights on the next benchmark: Reaching 1 million schoolchildren every day. She has every right, it seems, to be confident.
"From 25 kids to now, I feel like there's not one challenge that we haven't overcome."
The Prize is awarded by the German Africa Foundation (DAS), a nonpartisan foundation dedicated to promoting a nuanced view of Africa in political circles and among the German public.

Since 1993, it has awarded the German Africa Prize to individuals from African countries whose ideas and work inspire solutions to global issues of the future beyond their countries of origin. The award has gone to outstanding individuals in Zimbabwe, Cameroon and Sierra Leone in recent years.
German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan will present the German Africa Prize to Kenya's successful social entrepreneur on Wednesday evening.
German Africa Prize — Wawira Njiru reacts
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: BMW reports lower Q3 earnings as China woes mount
articles.summary: BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China.

image.caption: BMW set to ramp up restructuring measures (File: September 2026)Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter pretax earnings on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.
Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.

The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China. Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.
BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.
CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures."
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
The German carmaker lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.
Germany's auto industry struggling because of weak demand and competition from China
German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market, resulting in cost-cutting measures.
Volkswagen, the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.
BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?
The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October.

It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has announced that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.
On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.
According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.
German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.

articles.title: Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
articles.summary: The US imposed sanctions on Rwanda's army over its role in the conflict in DR Congo.

blocks.text: In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.
"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.
Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".
In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.
The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.
The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.
The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the African league in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.
Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.
The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.
DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.
It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

articles.title: Germany's celebrated children's author Janosch has died
articles.summary: Bear, Tiger and Tiger-Duck: The author and illustrator Janosch achieved world fame with his heartwarming children's figures. He died at the age of 95.

image.caption: Janosch standing next to his beloved characters, Bear and Tiger, in 2010Image: Roland Weihrauch/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals.
Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.

His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil announced on Wednesday.
Dismissed from arts school
Janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.
In 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent."

blocks.caption: This way to Panama: A sign in a bookstore featuring the author's famous illustrations Image: Uwe Zucchi/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: But luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.
His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.
Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.
The dream of a beautiful childhood

Even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him, but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.
Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.

He always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.

Janosch's animal figures are endearing, but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.
Janosch's path towards world fame

Janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.
Janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.

blocks.caption: The author next to a poster of 'Janosch's Dream World,' which was a TV series based on his booksImage: Horst Galuschka/IMAGO

blocks.text: There is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog. And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.
Merchandising with a Tiger-Duck

The "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.

His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.

blocks.caption: The Tiger-Duck character is a little wooden toy duck on wheels, with black and yellow stripes, shown here as a stuffed toyImage: Jörg Carstensen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'He who needs almost nothing, has everything'

Guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always said that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.

From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit, taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.
Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Miliband criticises Blair’s slavery statement and defends Burnham’s plan for proper apology – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The foreign secretary added that the UK will not shift its position on reparations

Good morning. Wednesdays are normally the most exciting day of the week at Westminster, because it’s PMQs,…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 2m agoBurnham says Commonwealth 'more important today than ever before'

blocks.text: Burnham says Commonwealth 'more important today than ever before'

Andy Burnham has described the Commonwealth as “more important today than ever before” amid “such volatile times”. He used the phrase in a meeting with his Antigua and Barbuda counterpart Gaston Browne, who is hosting the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).
In a readout of the meeting, released this morning, a No 10 spokesperson said:

double quotation markThe prime minister thanked Prime Minister Browne for the warm welcome from Antigua and Barbuda and for hosting Commonwealth leaders at such an important time. In such volatile times, it was clear that the Commonwealth was more important today than ever before, the prime minister added.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham (right) with Gaston Browne  ahead of a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Chogm. Photograph: Kin Cheung/PA

blocks.text: Good morning. Wednesdays are normally the most exciting day of the week at Westminster, because it’s PMQs, but today (unless we get some mega surprise) all the action is taking place somewhere else. In part, that’s because Andy Burnham is still at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. But mostly because anyone in SW1 with even a passing interest in politics will be far more interested in the outcome of the US midterm elections. You can catch up with all the drama on our US politics live blog.

While the US results are undoubtedly fascinating, quite how relevant they are to the UK is a bit harder to discern. Donald Trump is still president for the next two years, and none of the chaos he has caused for Britain and other European allies is going to go away; conceivably, he could end up even more disruptive. Trump was first elected president in 2016 only months after the UK voted for Brexit and there will be progressives in Britain hoping the US results show that what Ed Davey is this morning calling the “politics of hate, division and economic harm” might be on their way out this side of the pond too. Maybe? But it is probably too soon to get carried away. Our US coverage is all here. In so far as there is any interesting UK reaction, I will post it here.

Back to the Commonwealth summit, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has given an interview to the BBC in which he defended Burnham’s decision to open talks about a proper UK apology for slavery. In particular, Miliband was critical of Tony Blair’s attempts to settle this issue with what Miliband described as a “sorry not sorry” apology.

Miliband was referring to this statement that Blair issued in 2006, written up at the time by the Guardian here. Blair said the slave trade was “profoundly shameful” and he expressed “deep sorrow that it ever happened”. But he did not formally apologise.
In an interview with the BBC’s Newscast podcast, Miliband said Burnham wanted a different approach. He said:

double quotation markPeople have been honestly a bit bruised by the past, what happened in the past, the sense that we just really just wanted to sweep this issue under the carpet and not confront it. My sense is there’s a bit of a sigh of relief that, OK … at least there’s a sense of we’ve got a shared interest now in moving the Commonwealth on.
Miliband said Blair “did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation”. He added: “He kind of expressed ‘sorrow, but’ and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by No 10.”

(Miliband has for many years had a strained relationship with the former prime minister, who was opposed to the way Miliband criticised some aspects of New Labour’s record when he was party leader between 2010 and 2015. These latest remarks are just the latest example of feuding between the two of them.)

Burnham has said he wants a “structured dialogue” with Commonwealth countries about the wording of an apology. Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders’ summit in Manchester next November, Miliband said: “Broadly speaking, yes.”
But he also stressed that the UK was not offering reparations. Asked whether the government’s new approach could end up costing UK taxpayers a penny more, Miliband replied:

double quotation markNo … For us, that’s never been what it’s about. And that’s why it’s been important that … I did have this conversation with our partners in advance. I said, ‘Look, we are going to say we are willing to say that we’re open to an apology, but we’re not going to shift our position on reparations.’ It’s not for us. It’s not the right answer. It’s not practical. It’s not feasible for us, but there are things we can work on co-operatively.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, gives evidence to the Commons health committee.
10am: Lucy Powell, the education secretary, gives evidence to the Commons education committee.
Noon: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, faces Alex Burghart, the deputy Conservative leader, at PMQs.

articles.title: Four tankers destroyed by naval mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran's IRGC says
articles.summary: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says the vessels had hit sea mines while trying to cross a prohibited route.

blocks.text: Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval sea mines, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, a day after US officials said the US military had launched strikes on the country.

The IRGC said two of the vessels were still burning, and two additional tankers had been seized, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. It said they were trying to travel through a prohibited southern route in the Strait of Hormuz.

The BBC has not independently verified the IRGC's claim, which came as US voters punished Republicans at the midterm elections, leading Iran's top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, to say the results showed Americans had said no to war.
He warned Washington not to betray its public.
The IRCG also reported three tankers had been destroyed after hitting mines early on Tuesday, and that they had shot down an MQ-9 drone over the Strait.
The earlier US strikes on Qeshm were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's parliamentary speaker, posted on X, external that the midterm results showed that whether it was "conscience or the cost of living, Americans said no to war, and we endorse this message".
"If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our 'no' comes with a nightmare."

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday acknowledged the poor results for Republican congress members was partly due to the war on Iran and the consequent increased gas prices, but that he didn't regret launching it. He told the BBC's partner CBS News that the conflict would end "when I say it ends".

In an interview with the Financial Times ahead of the midterm elections on Tuesday, Trump suggested he was happy with the state of the conflict, and that he didn't consider them to be "really in a war".

Asked about comments by Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be another attack on Iran this week, Trump said they were "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".
On Tuesday night, Trump told Fox News there were some people who would "love" to do a "heavy hit" on Iran.
"The only thing I can tell you with certainty, they will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
Talks to end the conflict, which was triggered by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have been stalled for months, with little sign of a breakthrough.
Ghalibaf told a parliamentary session on Tuesday that Iran "will not surrender" and the responsibility to prevent a war lay with the US.

"If Washington makes another strategic mistake, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will be even more desperate than it is today as it searches for a way out," Ghalibaf said.
Meanwhile Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained his government had been trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue".
"No-one will benefit from this war" if fighting is restarted, he said on Tuesday.

Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to the attack, has said it will only reopen it if the US agrees to demands contained in its peace plan. Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei this week said the seven-step plan had been condensed, and could be implemented in two days if the US agreed.

articles.title: Delhi air quality worsens ahead of Diwali as firework restrictions enter force
articles.summary: On Wednesday morning, Delhi's air quality index reading stood at 377, in the "very poor" category.

blocks.text: Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality.

The city's Air Quality Index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.
Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.
Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.
Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.
The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.

The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.
The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.
Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.
A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, north-westerly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.
India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.
The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.
With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.
Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.
Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.
On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.
It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.
The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.

Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.
But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.
In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.
It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.
During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.

The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.

On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.
The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.
The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.

articles.title: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments: What's happened so far in the midterms
articles.summary: Democrats have taken control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency - proving moments of celebration.

blocks.text: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments: What's happened so far in the midterms
How the Democratic takeover of the Senate could impact Trump
ByNardine Saad
Reporting fromLos Angeles, California
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Even before results are finalised, the night has provided some historic results and scenes of celebration. These are some of the key moments so far.
Democrats talk of 'great American comeback' after historic results

Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Republican President Trump two years ago, registering sizeable swings in the likes of Texas, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina.

Among the senior party figures who have cheered the results are Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.
"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.
If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Jeffries.
Trump congratulates opposition on 'good job'
Trump has spoken throughout the night to a number of media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".

He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Texas.

Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."
Cheers as Democrats win first Senate flip of the night in North Carolina

blocks.caption: Image caption, Roy Cooper was expected to have a tough fight on his hands in North Carolina

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Roy Cooper was expected to have a tough fight on his hands in North Carolina
There were cheers from supporters in North Carolina as the Democrats secured the night's first flip of a Senate seat.
The state's former Democratic governor, Roy Cooper, won against Republican candidate Michael Whatley.
"Tonight we show the country that when everyday people come together, we can make change," Cooper said as he addressed his supporters on Tuesday.
The last time the Democrats won a Senate race in the state was 2008, despite the party making enormous investment in time and money behind their candidates in recent contests.
Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes first black female governor

blocks.caption: Image caption, Keisha Lance Bottoms beat billionaire businessman Rick Jackson,

blocks.text: Keisha Lance Bottoms beat billionaire businessman Rick Jackson,

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, has been projected to win the governor's race in Georgia, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.
The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue, which came after the state's former senator said the party was "nauseously optimistic" about their chances this year.

Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive, who was endorsed by outgoing Governor Brian Kemp and President Trump, who spent $200 million of his own money on the race.
The state has also not had a Democratic governor in more than 20 years.
Ossoff victory in Georgia adds fuel to 2028 speculation

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jon Ossoff as seen as a potential future Democratic contender for the presidency

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Jon Ossoff as seen as a potential future Democratic contender for the presidency
As well as Bottoms being elected the new governor of Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff has been projected as the winner of the Senate race there, giving him a second term.
His victory was not unexpected as he had a comfortable lead in the polls over his Republican challenger Mike Collins - a member of the lower House chamber.
Ossoff told his supporters following his victory that for those who "doubted whether our republic would survive" over the last two years, the "first light of dawn is on the horizon".

Republicans had hoped this would be a more competitive race because the Peach State has been reliably Republican for decades. Trump also won it in the 2024 presidential election, after Joe Biden eked out a narrow victory there in 2020.

Now that he has won re-election in the Senate, the speculation surrounding Ossoff's plans for the next presidential election in 2028 will likely increase - he is considered a potential leading contender if he throws his hat in the ring.
Chris Pappas celebrates with husband as first openly gay man elected to Senate
Watch: "I am ready to fight" - Senator-elect Chris Pappas celebrates New Hampshire win
Democrat Chris Pappas has also made history as the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.
Pappas is projected to defeat former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race - who comes from one of the state's political dynasties having seen his father and brother serve as governor.

But the contest between the two was well-natured, with Pappas thanking his opponent on Tuesday by saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."
The 46-year-old Pappas had represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 but chose not to run for re-election so he could launch his campaign for the Senate.

articles.title: From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated
articles.summary: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find…

image.caption: From rotten food and sexual behavior to political beliefs, researchers want to know how different forms of disgust relate to our attitudesImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.
One explanation begins with evolution.
"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.
What are the three types of disgust?
But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

items: Pathogen disgust: Reactions to potential sources of infection, such as rotten food, vomit or bodily waste.
Sexual disgust: Reactions to particular sexual behaviors or situations.
Moral disgust: Reactions to wrongdoing, such as betrayal or cruelty. Researchers debate whether this reflects physical revulsion or moral disapproval.

blocks.text: One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump used language evoking contagion when describing immigrants early in his 2024 presidential campaignImage: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.
"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."
Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.
"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.
Do liberals and conservatives feel disgust differently?
Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.
A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.
However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.
Can our bodies reveal our politics?
Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.
Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged
But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.
Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.
"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.
How do gut feelings influence political beliefs?
Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.
"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."
The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."
They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.
But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.
What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

blocks.caption: Pathogen disgust is one type of disgust thought to have evolved to protect us from infectionImage: Elena Shishkina/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: "People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.
Can disgust actually be measured?
Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.
He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.
Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.
"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.
The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.
Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."
How might politicians exploit feelings of disgust?
Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.
"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.
Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?
"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.
Does disgust influence how people vote?

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.
"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.
Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.
"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."
Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.
He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.
"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said.

articles.title: How America voted in maps and charts
articles.summary: See the maps and charts that show how America voted in the US midterm elections.

blocks.text: How America voted in maps and charts
ByWesley Stephenson
Data Journalist
It's been an extraordinary night for the Democrats so far in the US midterms.
They have taken control of the Senate and are projected to take control of the House of Representatives too, according to the BBC's partner CBS News.
Senate

The results in the Senate are beyond what the Democrats would have expected. North Carolina was a likely pick-up but South Carolina was a huge shock and Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932.
Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine have also turned blue. There is one toss-up seat to come in Alaska and even Mississippi is now on a knife edge, according to CBS News.
Polls before the election saw South Carolina as leaning Republican. It had been a deep red seat for many years, last returning a Democratic senator in 1998.
House

The BBC's partner CBS News projected the Democrats would win the House just after 03:00 GMT on Wednesday (22:00 EST Tuesday). The Democrats are making the gains they need to take control but have their sights set on a much bigger victory.
Two significant seats are Florida 14 and Florida 25 which the Democrats have held. This is a blow to the Republicans' attempt to redraw the boundaries in their favour.
The redistricting saw both districts move from having a majority of 2024 Kamala Harris voters to having a majority of people who voted for Donald Trump.
Florida 22, which was also redrawn to favour the Republicans, saw a victory for the Democrats too.
Hispanic voters turn to Democrats in Florida

Hispanic voters look to be one of the key groups in the elections in Florida. A huge poll of voters suggests that this group backed the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon by 55% to 44% for the Republican Ashley Moody.
This is a turnaround from the estimated 55% of Hispanic voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024.
The poll also asked what issues voters were most concerned about. It suggests that across the country the economy was the biggest issue, followed by the state of democracy.
When voters were asked if Donald Trump's policies impacted economic conditions, the poll suggests more that two-thirds believe they had made things worse.
Produced by Wesley Stephenson, Christine Jeavans, Daniel Wainwright, Becky Dale, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, John Walton and Rob England.

articles.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
articles.summary:
Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts

The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s…

blocks.text: The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls show it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.
Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.

Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.

blocks.caption: An ANC poster in Langa township in Cape Town. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters

blocks.text: Johannesburg, Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are in Gauteng, South Africa’s most populous and densely populated province and its economic engine. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance is leading the polls in all three metros but has not been polling above 40%.

The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs with a combination of the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters and the populist Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA across the province’s three metros.

blocks.caption: Helen Zille is campaigning to become mayor of Johannesburg. Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPA

blocks.text: In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to controversial past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.

The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.

blocks.caption: Jacob Zuma addresses an election rally in KwaMashu, north of Durban, on Sunday. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma is polling above 40%. The 84-year-old Zuma, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.
The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.

South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

articles.title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats eye sweeping gains and reshaping of political map
articles.summary: Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds turned out to be slam-dunks for the Democrats.

blocks.text: This is already shaping up to be a very good night for Democrats, with much of the vote counted in the eastern United States and polls closing in key Midwestern battleground states.

Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds have turned out to be slam dunks for the Democrats - Jon Ossoff's re-election race in Georgia and the open Republican-held seat in North Carolina.

That North Carolina contest, where former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper bested Republican Party insider Michael Whatley, was the first of the four pick-ups Democrats need in order to wrest control of the Senate.
Attention has now turned to Republican-held Senate seats in Texas, Kansas and Ohio, where counting is taking place.
In South Carolina, the BBC's US partner CBS News is rating the Senate race as leaning Democrat, which would be an earth-shaking result.
If you look at key races in House of Representatives, there are other encouraging signs for Democrats.
In Florida, Republicans in the state legislature had redrawn the boundaries of three Democratic-held seats to make it much easier to for them to win.
They lost all three.

items: US midterm elections results 2026
Live updates

blocks.text: Other House races in the state, where Republicans expected to win by comfortable margins, have turned out to be dogfights.
Democrats flipped an open seat in western North Carolina, for instance, and appear in position to make gains in Virginia, Kentucky and Indiana.
In races considered toss-ups across the east, Democrats are poised for the kind of victories that will help secure a House majority for the first time since 2022.
They're doing it on the back of high Democratic turnout, particularly by black voters in the south, and winning back Hispanic voters in Florida who had supported the Republicans just two years ago.
In majority black South Carolina counties, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews is significantly outperforming Kamala Harris's presidential numbers in 2024.
And in Miami-Dade County, which Trump carried that year, Democratic candidates are back on top.

articles.title: ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
articles.summary: As South Africans vote in local elections, residents tell the BBC they are tired of the poor quality of services they get.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
More than 500 parties are contesting the elections
ByKhanyisile Ngcobo
Reporting fromJohannesburg
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's former ruling party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.

For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.

The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his vote

blocks.text: Image source, Khanyisile Ngcobo/BBC
Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his vote
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of decline

blocks.text: The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of decline
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.

Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.

A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".

"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.

Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.

blocks.caption: Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd is seen smiling with a denim jacket

blocks.text: Melanie Verwoerd
The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done

blocks.caption: "The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done", Source: Melanie Verwoerd, Source description: Political analyst, Image: Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd is seen smiling with a denim jacket

blocks.text: Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
But that might change.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.

The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.
DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.

The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".
She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".
Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.

These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the years

blocks.text: Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the years
Verwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.

Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.
Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.

The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.
The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.
Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.
A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.
Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros.
"We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.

Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.

Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.
South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.
